metadata.scope: e_turan (all baronies across k_transoxiana, k_oghuz_il, k_khotan, and k_syr_darya)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_charkliq.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Turkic/Uyghur name Charkliq (Qakilik); the oasis was recorded as Nafubo by Xuanzang in 645 CE and earlier associated with Ruoqiang/Wuni in the Book of Han.
b_charkliq.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Çarqiliq / Charkliq (conventionally derived from čarq 'wheel' + -liq, or a local Turkic adaptation of an older Tarim toponym), replacing earlier Han-Tang names Ruoqiang and Nafubo.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (645 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Aurel Stein identified Xuanzang's 645 CE Na-fu-bo (納縛波) with the Charklik oasis.

b_bashkoyumal.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the modern Uyghur name Bashkoyumal; the ruined fort and stupa 5 miles south of Charklik yielded a 6th-century CE Sanskrit silk manuscript and Tang-era occupation.
b_bashkoyumal.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur local designation Bash-Koyumal recorded by Aurel Stein in 1907 for a ruined early-Tang Buddhist fort and stupa south of Charklik.

b_waxxari.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the name Waxxari (Washixia); Waxxari Township was formally established in 1953.
b_waxxari.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Waxxari (Vash-shahri, Chinese Washixia 瓦石峡), a modern town in Ruoqiang County along the southern Silk Road oasis chain.

b_miran.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the modern name Miran; the site was known as Yixun/Yuni in Han sources (1st century BCE) and Nob Chungu in Tibetan documents (mid-8th to mid-9th century CE).
b_miran.etymology_analysis: Modern local name Mirān for the abandoned ancient oasis city and Tibetan fort on the southern rim of the Taklamakan Desert.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (1st century BCE) for Yixun; 8th–9th century CE Tibetan woodslips for Nob Chungu
older_name_by_867.notes: Han agricultural/military colony Yixun (伊循, 77 BCE) and later Tibetan fort Nob Chungu (Little Nob, mid-8th to mid-9th century CE).

b_omotrunnaisse.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE (or in standard historical/modern gazetteers) found for Omotrunnaisse.
b_omotrunnaisse.etymology_analysis: Unattested toponym in the Miran/Dunhuang sector with no identifiable historical or linguistic record.

b_dunhuang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Shiji and Book of Han (Hanshu) when Emperor Wu of Han established Dunhuang Commandery in 111 BCE.
b_dunhuang.etymology_analysis: Chinese Dūnhuáng (敦煌, 'grand and blazing'), likely a Han-era phonetic transcription of an earlier non-Chinese (Yuezhi or Qiang) toponym reinterpreted with auspicious Chinese characters.

b_nanhu_TARIM.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Mandarin Chinese name Nanhu ('South Lake') in the Dunhuang/Yangguan oasis.
b_nanhu_TARIM.etymology_analysis: Chinese Nánhú (南湖, 'South Lake'), a modern oasis and lake name near Yangguan southwest of Dunhuang.

b_karashar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Turkic-Persian name Karashar (Qarashähär); the oasis was known as Yanqi in Han-Tang Chinese sources (1st century BCE) and Ārśi/Agni in Tocharian A and Sanskrit.
b_karashar.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Qarashähär / Karashar ('Black City' or 'Great City'), a post-867 Turkic-Persian compound replacing ancient Yanqi / Ārśi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (1st century BCE) for Yanqi; Tocharian A manuscripts (7th century CE) for Ārśi
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient oasis kingdom recorded as Yanqi (焉耆) in Han Chinese chronicles and Ārśi (Sanskrit Agni) in Tocharian A texts.

b_bosten.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Mongolic name Bosten (Bostang); in Han-Tang Chinese sources the lake was called Xihai ('Western Sea').
b_bosten.etymology_analysis: Bosten (Chinese Bositeng 博斯騰), from Oirat/Chagatai Bostang ('oasis/garden'), a post-867 name for the largest freshwater lake in Xinjiang (known in Uyghur as Baghrash Köli).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Han-era Chinese geographical records (Book of Han / Shuijingzhu)
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in ancient Chinese sources as Xīhǎi (西海, 'Western Sea') prior to the Mongolic/Uyghur names Bosten and Baghrash.

b_narinkira.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the name Narinkira.
b_narinkira.etymology_analysis: Turkic-Mongolic compound Narinkira (narin 'narrow' + qyr 'ridge/edge'), unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_korla.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the name Korla (Kurla); during the Han and Three Kingdoms eras the oasis was recorded as Yuli (尉犁).

morphemes.translation: modern oasis name (possibly related to Kroran/Kurla)

b_korla.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Korla / Kurla (Chinese Kù'ěrlè 庫爾勒), a post-867 toponym for the oasis known in Han-Wei sources as Yuli.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (1st century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Recorded in the Book of Han (125 BCE–23 CE) as the oasis statelet of Yuli (尉犁).

b_kongque.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Kongque ('Peacock' River); the Chinese name is a modern folk-etymological rendering of Uyghur Konchi Darya ('Tanner's River').

morphemes.language: Mandarin Chinese (phonetic adaptation of Uyghur konchi 'tanner')

b_kongque.etymology_analysis: Chinese Kǒngquè Hé (孔雀河, 'Peacock River'), a semantically distorted modern transliteration of Uyghur Konchi Darya ('Tanner's River').

b_kucha.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (1st century BCE) as Qiuci (龜茲) and in Tocharian B / Sanskrit sources (4th–7th centuries CE) as Kuśi / Kuci.
b_kucha.etymology_analysis: Modern Kucha (Uyghur Kuchar, Chinese Kuche/Qiuci) directly continues the Tocharian B endonym Kuśi / Kuci, attested since the Han dynasty.

b_jigdalik.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Uyghur name Jigdalik (recorded as an archaeological site near Kucha in early 20th-century surveys).
b_jigdalik.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Jigdälik ('place of oleaster trees'), a modern Turkic toponym for a ruined site in the Kucha region.

b_duldulokur.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Islamic-era folk name Duldulokur (Duldul-akhur), though the Buddhist ruins at the site date to Tang times (8th century CE).
b_duldulokur.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Duldul-okur from Persian Duldul-ākhur ('manger of Duldul'), a post-Islamization folk name applied to Tang-era Buddhist monastery ruins southwest of Kucha.

b_toksu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Toksu; Toksu County (later renamed Xinhe) was created from Kuqa in 1930.
b_toksu.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Toqsu ('abundant water' or contracted from toqquz su 'nine waters'), the historical Uyghur name of Xinhe County near Kucha.

b_shayar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Shayar (Xayar); Xayar County was established in 1902.
b_shayar.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Shayar / Xayar (Chinese Shāyǎ 沙雅), a modern oasis county south of Kucha in Aksu Prefecture.

b_luntai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Shiji and Book of Han during Li Guangli's Fergana campaign in 101 BCE, followed by a Han military colony around 80 BCE.
b_luntai.etymology_analysis: Chinese Lúntái (輪台, 'wheel terrace'), a Han-era phonetic rendering of an indigenous Tarim oasis name.

b_bugur_TARIM.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Mongolic/Uyghur name Bugur (Bügür); the county was known in Han times as Luntai (101 BCE) and Wulei (60 BCE).
b_bugur_TARIM.etymology_analysis: Mongolic/Uyghur Bügür (Chinese Bùgǔ'ěr 布古爾), the post-867 name for Luntai County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (establishment of Protectorate of the Western Regions in 60 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: In 60 BCE, the Han dynasty established the Protectorate of the Western Regions at Wulei (烏壘) in present-day Luntai/Bügür County.

b_subashi.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Turkic/Uyghur name Subashi; the Buddhist monastery ruins at the site were described by Xuanzang in 630 CE under the name Zhaohuli.
b_subashi.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Su Bashi ('headwaters / head of the water'), a post-867 Turkic toponym for the ruined ancient Buddhist temple complex north of Kucha.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (c. 630 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The Subashi Buddhist ruins correspond to the twin Zhaohuli (昭怙釐) monasteries visited by Xuanzang in 630 CE.

b_shorchuk.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Uyghur name Shorchuk (Xorqu); the Buddhist temple site (Qigexing / Shikshin) flourished in the 5th–10th centuries CE.
b_shorchuk.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Xorqu / Šorčuq ('salty place'), referring to salt deposits in the steppes around the ancient Buddhist monastery ruins southwest of Karashahr.

b_nasi_erkule.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the name Nasi Erkule.
b_nasi_erkule.etymology_analysis: Modern/obscure Turkic-Uyghur toponym in the Luntai region containing köl ('lake'), unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_toksun.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Turkic/Uyghur name Toksun ('ninety').
b_toksun.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Toqsun (from Turkic toqsan 'ninety', likely a distance or station designation), a post-867 oasis town in the Turpan Depression.

b_bezeklik.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Uyghur name Bezeklik; the cave complex dates from the 5th–14th centuries CE (mostly West Uyghur Kingdom, 10th–13th centuries).
b_bezeklik.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Bezeklik ('decorated place' / 'place with paintings'), a post-867 name for the Buddhist cave temples in the Mutou Valley near Turpan.

b_sengim.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Uyghur name Sengim (Sängim).

morphemes.translation: local gorge/village name in Turpan (Chinese Shengjin)

b_sengim.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Sängim / Sengim (Chinese Shengjin 勝金), a valley and village near Karakhoja/Turpan known for Manichaean and Buddhist cave remains.

b_kashgar.first_mention_attestation: No undisputed written attestation <= 867 CE found for the compound name Kashgar (Kāshghar, first solidly attested in 10th-century Islamic sources such as Hudud al-'Alam, 982 CE); earlier records call it Shule (Book of Han, 1st century BCE) and Kasha (Xuanzang, 644 CE).
b_kashgar.etymology_analysis: Kāshghar (Uyghur Qäshqär); H. W. Bailey proposed an Eastern Iranian compound from Kāš + -ğar ('mountain'), though Encyclopaedia Iranica notes no etymology is firmly established.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (125 BCE–23 CE) for Shule; Xuanzang (644 CE) for Kasha
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in Han-Tang Chinese sources as Shule (疏勒) and to Xuanzang in the 7th century as Kasha (佉沙).

b_yopurga.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Yopurga; recorded in Qing times as Yopurga Zhuang and made a county in 1943.
b_yopurga.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Yopurgha (Chinese Yuèpǔhú 岳普湖), named after the Yopurga River in the western Tarim Basin.

b_yengi_xahar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the Qing 'new city' of Shule (Uyghur Yëngi Sheher / Yengi Xahar) was constructed in 1828 CE.
b_yengi_xahar.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Yëngi Shähär / Yengi Xahar ('New City'), referring to the Qing-era Han garrison town of Shule built 6 miles southeast of Old Kashgar.

b_kona_xahar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Uyghur name Kona Xahar ('Old City', Shufu County).
b_kona_xahar.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Kona Shähär / Kona Xahar ('Old City'), the Qing/modern Uyghur name for Shufu County adjacent to Kashgar.

b_akto.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Kyrgyz name Akto ('White Mountain').
b_akto.etymology_analysis: Kyrgyz Aq-too ('White Mountain'), referring to the snow-capped Pamir peaks overlooking the oasis.

b_maralbeshi.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Uyghur name Maralbeshi; Maralbexi County was established in 1913.
b_maralbeshi.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Maralbëshi ('Deer Head'), a post-867 toponym for the oasis in the Kashgar/Yarkand river valley.

b_atus.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the name Atus / Artush; Artush becomes prominent in the 10th-century Kara-Khanid era (mausoleum of Satuk Bughra Khan, d. 955 CE).
b_atus.etymology_analysis: Uyghur Artush / Atush (Chinese Ātúshí 阿圖什), attested from the Kara-Khanid period (10th–11th centuries CE) onward.

b_terek.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Kyrgyz/Turkic name Terek (Terek Pass / Terek-davan).
b_terek.etymology_analysis: Kyrgyz/Turkic Terek ('poplar'), naming the Terek-davan mountain pass linking Kashgar and the Fergana Valley.

b_ulugqat.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Kyrgyz/Uyghur name Ulugqat (Wuqia).
b_ulugqat.etymology_analysis: Kyrgyz/Uyghur Ulugh-chat ('great gorge' or 'great confluence'), a post-867 toponym in Kizilsu Prefecture (Chinese Wuqia 烏恰).

b_yarkand.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Turkic and Islamic sources, first in Mahmud al-Kashgari's Diwan Lughat al-Turk (1072–1074 CE) and 11th-century CE Qarakhanid coins and legal documents as Yarkand.
b_yarkand.etymology_analysis: Compound toponym attested from the 11th century CE, composed of Turkic yar ('cliff, steep riverbank, gorge') and the Eastern Iranian urban suffix -känd ('town, settlement', borrowed into Turkic).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) recording the kingdom of Shache/Suoju (Old Chinese *sˤa(j)-ka, likely related to the Saka ethnonym).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Saka oasis kingdom on the southern Silk Road, recorded in Han and Tang Chinese chronicles before adopting the Turkic-Iranian name Yarkand by the 11th century CE.

b_yengisar.first_mention_attestation: Late 15th-century CE Chaghatayid-era historical records (1499 CE, when Ahmad Alaq seized Kashgar and Yengisar from Mirza Abu Bakr Dughlat, as Yangi Hissar / Yengisar).
b_yengisar.etymology_analysis: Uyghur contraction of Yangi Hissar ('New Fortress'), combining Turkic yängi ('new') with Perso-Arabic hisār ('fortress, walled town').

b_makit.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; the modern oasis and county of Makit (Markit/Merket) is attested in 20th-century CE administrative records (county established 1928 CE).

morphemes.translation: oasis town on the Yarkand River

b_makit.etymology_analysis: Uyghur toponym (also transliterated Markit, Mekit, Merket; Chinese Maigaiti) on the lower Yarkand River, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation; often linked to the medieval Merkit ethnonym.

b_cherchen.first_mention_attestation: Late 13th-century CE travelogue of Marco Polo (c. 1273 CE, as Ciarcian / Charchan) and 16th-century CE Chaghatayid sources (Mirza Haidar as Jurjan).

morphemes.translation: oasis town on the Cherchen River (possibly from Shanshan/Calmadana)

b_cherchen.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur and Europeanized toponym (Qarqan / Charchan / Cherchen), possibly derived via phonetic shift from the ancient kingdom name Shanshan or Kharoshthi Calmadana; first attested in this form in the late 13th century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) as Qiemo; 3rd-century CE Kharoshthi documents of Kroraina as Calmadana; Xuanzang (644 CE) as Zhemotuona; Tang Annals (after 674 CE) as Boxian Zhen.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient oasis state of Qiemo/Calmadana on the southern Silk Road, annexed by Shanshan/Kroraina in the Han period and garrisoned by the Tang as Boxian Zhen.

b_saca.first_mention_attestation: 3rd-century CE Gandhari Prakrit documents in Kharoshthi script from the Kingdom of Kroraina (e.g., Document no. 14), explicitly naming Saca as a guarded station between Calmadana (Cherchen) and Nina (Niya).
b_saca.etymology_analysis: Ancient oasis toponym attested in 3rd-century CE Kharoshthi administrative tablets of Kroraina as Saca, tentatively identified with the Endere ruins between Cherchen and Niya (possibly connected to the Saka ethnonym).

b_endere.first_mention_attestation: Modern archaeological and local Uyghur name recorded during Sir Aurel Stein's 1901 CE excavation of the Endere fort and Buddhist shrine.

morphemes.translation: desert oasis and ruined fort site between Niya and Cherchen

b_endere.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur name for the ruined Silk Road fort and Buddhist site (Chinese Andi'er) excavated by Aurel Stein in 1901 CE. The ancient site flourished under the Han and Tang (tentatively identified with Kharoshthi Saca, represented by b_saca) before its 9th-century CE abandonment.

b_dondan_oilik.first_mention_attestation: Rediscovered and recorded in 1896 CE by Swedish explorer Sven Hedin from the local Uyghur designation Dandan Oilik ('houses with ivory'); the ancient town was abandoned in the late 8th century CE.
b_dondan_oilik.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur name (Dandān-Uiliq, literally 'the houses with ivory', combining Persian dandān 'tooth/ivory' and Uyghur öylük 'houses/dwellings'), recorded by Sven Hedin in 1896 CE for a Buddhist oasis town abandoned in the late 8th century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 8th-century CE Tang-era Chinese and Khotanese documents from the site (identified in Sven Hedin's Central Asia Atlas as Li-hsieh).
older_name_by_867.notes: Flourished from the 6th to late 8th century CE as a Buddhist oasis town under Khotanese and Tang administration (Li-hsieh) before abandonment prior to the Tibetan advance.

b_laodamogou.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern Chinese archaeological designation (Lao Damagou, 'Old Damagou') for ruined Buddhist sites in the Damagou oasis of Qira County.

morphemes.language: Chinese transcription of Sanskrit Dharma + Khotanese -kho

b_laodamogou.etymology_analysis: Modern Chinese designation meaning 'Old Damagou', where Damagou (local oasis/ditch name) is traditionally derived from Sanskrit Dharma plus a Khotanese locative suffix -kho ('place where Buddhist teachings gather').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) and Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (644 CE) for the ancient oasis state of Pimo/Bimo in the Damagou–Domoko region.
older_name_by_867.notes: The Damagou area formed part of the ancient oasis state of Pimo (Bimo) during the Han dynasty before absorption into Khotan.

b_mahas.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern geographical/archaeological site name (also spelled Mohas) in the southern Tarim Basin between Damagou and Dandan Oilik.

morphemes.translation: abandoned oasis ruin site in the Khotan–Qira desert

b_mahas.etymology_analysis: Modern local toponym (also rendered Mohas in Chinese geographical surveys of the southern Tarim Basin) for an abandoned desert ruin site near Damagou, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_karghalik.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found for the Turkic name Karghalik (Qaghiliq); attested in post-medieval Central Asian and Qing-era records, whereas pre-867 CE sources record earlier names for the oasis.
b_karghalik.etymology_analysis: Turkic (Uyghur) toponym Qaghiliq / Karghalik, formed from qarğa ('crow') and the locative/abundance suffix -lıq ('place of crows'), postdating the pre-Islamic Saka/Chinese names of the oasis.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) as Xiye; Song Yun (519 CE) as Zhujuban; Xuanzang (644 CE) as Zhegujia/Chakuka.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient oasis kingdom on the southern Silk Road, recorded in Han, Wei, and Tang Buddhist pilgrim accounts before Turkification.

b_guma.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found for the name Guma (Goma); attested in Qing-era and modern records (19th century CE), whereas Han-era sources call the oasis Pishan.

morphemes.translation: oasis town between Khotan and Karghalik

b_guma.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur toponym (Guma / Goma) for the oasis town officially known in Chinese as Pishan; the name Guma is unattested before 867 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) recording the oasis state of Pishan.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient caravan hub on the route from Khotan toward the Karakoram and Pamirs, conquered by Khotan in the 1st century CE.

b_kehan.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern Chinese geographical/archaeological designation (Kehan) for a ruined desert site near Pishan in the southwestern Tarim Basin.

morphemes.translation: abandoned oasis site in the southwestern Tarim Basin

b_kehan.etymology_analysis: Modern Chinese-transcribed name of an abandoned ancient settlement site near Pishan and Mazartag in the southwestern Tarim Basin, lacking any documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_keriya.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found for the name Keriya; attested in Qing-era and modern records (18th–19th century CE), whereas Han-era sources used Yumi and Marco Polo used Pem/Peyn.
b_keriya.etymology_analysis: Uyghur toponym (Kériyä) derived from the Keriya River flowing north from the Kunlun Mountains into the Taklamakan Desert; the name Keriya itself is unattested before 867 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Zhang Qian's embassy report (125 BCE) and Book of Han (Hanshu) recording the oasis kingdom of Yumi (later Jumi/Ningmi) on the Keriya River.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Silk Road kingdom on the Keriya River, associated with the archaeological sites of Yuansha and Karadong.

b_andir.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern local toponym (Andir / Andi'er, attested in 20th-century CE Xinjiang administrative and geographical records) along the Andir River.

morphemes.translation: desert oasis and river station in Minfeng County

b_andir.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur toponym (Chinese Andi'er) for a desert pasture and archaeological zone in Minfeng (Niya) County, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_niya.first_mention_attestation: Modern Uyghur name Niya (Chinese Niya), recorded in early 20th-century CE geographical and archaeological accounts (Aurel Stein, 1900 CE); derived from earlier Nina / Nizhang.

morphemes.translation: oasis town on the Niya River

b_niya.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur form of the ancient oasis name Nina (3rd-century CE Kharoshthi) and Tang-era Nizhang (644 CE), located 115 km south of the ancient Caḍ́ota (Jingjue) ruins.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) as Jingjue; 3rd-century CE Kharoshthi tablets as Caḍ́ota and Nina; Xuanzang (644 CE) as Nizhang.
older_name_by_867.notes: Major oasis kingdom of Jingjue/Caḍ́ota on the southern Silk Road, absorbed into Shanshan/Kroraina by the 3rd century CE.

b_khotan.first_mention_attestation: 2nd-century BCE Chinese records (Zhang Qian's report, c. 125 BCE, in Shiji and Hanshu as Yutian, transcribing *Godana/*Khotana), 3rd-century CE Kharoshthi documents as Khotana, and Khotanese Saka manuscripts as Hvatana.
b_khotan.etymology_analysis: Ancient Saka and Prakrit toponym (Khotana, Khotanese Hvatana, Sanskritized as Gosthana/Kustana 'land of cows' or 'breast of the earth', Chinese Yutian), continuously attested since the 2nd century BCE.

b_lafak.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern local name (Lafak) for a ruined ancient settlement site in the Khotan oasis.

morphemes.translation: abandoned settlement site in the Khotan oasis

b_lafak.etymology_analysis: Modern local toponym for an abandoned ancient oasis site in the Khotan region, recorded in Chinese geographical surveys of southern Tarim Basin ruins without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_bugaiwilik.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern Uyghur/local name (Bugaiwilik) for an abandoned oasis ruin site in the Khotan region.

morphemes.translation: abandoned settlement site in the Khotan oasis

b_bugaiwilik.etymology_analysis: Modern local Uyghur toponym (with -wilik/-öylük, 'houses/settlement') for an abandoned ancient site in the Khotan oasis, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_domoko.first_mention_attestation: Modern Uyghur village and oasis name (Domoko), recorded in early 20th-century CE archaeological surveys (Aurel Stein) after the old village was abandoned in the mid-19th century CE.
b_domoko.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur oasis name east of Khotan (near the Damagou/Toplukdong Buddhist ruins); the name Domoko itself has no documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_yuetgan.first_mention_attestation: Modern Uyghur village name (Yotkan / Yuetgan), recorded in late 19th- and early 20th-century CE archaeological surveys (Sven Hedin, Aurel Stein) at the site of the ancient Khotanese capital.

morphemes.translation: ancient capital site near modern Khotan

b_yuetgan.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur name for the archaeological site 8 km west of modern Hotan, likely preserving a local phonetic reflex of Yutian/Hvatana; first documented under this form in 19th-century CE exploration.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu, 1st–2nd century CE) naming Xicheng ('Western City') as the main urban center of Yutian (Khotan).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient urban center of the Kingdom of Khotan; distinct from the kingdom/city name Khotan/Yutian (b_khotan).

b_dafang.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found for the name Dafang (short for modern Dafangpancheng, 'Great Square-Plate City'); the Han-era military granary at the site was known as Hecang.
b_dafang.etymology_analysis: Shortened form of modern Chinese Dafangpancheng ('Great Square-Plate City'), a descriptive modern name for the rectangular Han-Jin rammed-earth military granary near Yumen Pass.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Han dynasty military frontier records (c. 104 BCE–420 CE) designating the Yumen Pass granary complex as Hecang.
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-Wei-Jin military supply warehouse located 11 km northwest of Yumen Pass on the Shule River.

b_shule_river.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found for the Gansu river under the name Shule River (Shule He); in Tang times it was known as Jishui, while Shule originally referred to Kashgar.
b_shule_river.etymology_analysis: Hydronym denoting the second-largest inland river of Gansu (Shule He), flowing past Yumen Pass toward the Lop Nur basin; the name Shule is unattested for this river before 867 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tang-era geographical records referring to the river course north of Dunhuang/Yumen Pass as Jishui.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient endorheic river of the western Hexi Corridor draining toward Lop Nur.

b_kumtag.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; the Turkic toponym Kumtag (Qumtağ, 'sand mountain') was recorded in 19th-century CE geographical exploration (Vladimir Obruchev, 1894 CE).
b_kumtag.etymology_analysis: Turkic (Uyghur) compound Qumtağ ('sand mountain'), referring to the hyper-arid sand-dune desert southeast of Lop Nur.

b_turin_TARIM.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern Chinese-transcribed name (Turin) for an abandoned ancient site near Loulan and Miran in the Lop Nur basin.

morphemes.translation: abandoned desert site near Lop Nur

b_turin_TARIM.etymology_analysis: Modern geographical designation (Turin) for an abandoned ancient oasis site in the Lop Nur–Miran area, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_loulan.first_mention_attestation: 2nd-century BCE Chinese historical records (Zhang Qian's report of 126 BCE and Sima Qian's Shiji, c. 91 BCE) as Loulan, transcribing the indigenous name Kroraina.

morphemes.translation: ancient oasis kingdom and city near Lop Nur

b_loulan.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription (Lóulán) of the indigenous Tocharian/Krorainic name Kroraina (Kroran), attested from 126 BCE in Han sources; renamed Shanshan in 77 BCE while the Lop Nur city retained the name Loulan.

b_tikenik.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern Uyghur settlement name (Tikenlik / Tieganlik) on the lower Tarim River in Ruoqiang County.
b_tikenik.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur toponym Tikenlik (spelled Tikenik here, Chinese Tieganlike), formed from tikän ('thorn') and -lik ('place of'), denoting a town on the lower Tarim River.

b_argan.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern local toponym (Argan / Arghan) on the lower reaches of the Tarim River between the Taklamakan and Kuruk Tagh.

morphemes.translation: lower Tarim River station and desert locality

b_argan.etymology_analysis: Modern local toponym (Argan / Arghan) in the lower Tarim River floodplain between Tikenlik and Lop Nur, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_chelik.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern local toponym (Chelik) in the Lop Nur / lower Tarim region.

morphemes.translation: locality in the Lop Nur–Tarim region

b_chelik.etymology_analysis: Modern local toponym (Chelik) in the Lop Nur / lower Tarim Basin, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_aksu_mongolia.first_mention_attestation: Post-867 CE Turkic toponym Aksu (Aqsu, 'white water'), documented by the Mongol era (1207–1208 CE submission to Genghis Khan); earlier Han–Tang sources called the oasis Gumo and Baluka.
b_aksu_mongolia.etymology_analysis: Turkic (Uyghur) hydronym Aqsu ('white water', from aq 'white' + su 'water'), transferred from the Aksu River to the oasis city (adapted in the repo as Middle High German Wîzenflôz, 'white river/flow').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) as Gumo; Xuanzang (629 CE) as Baluka (Sanskrit Bharuka).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Tocharian-speaking oasis kingdom of Gumo/Bharuka on the northern Silk Road, contested by Tang China, Tibet, and the Uyghurs before adopting the Turkic name Aksu.

b_barchuk.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; medieval and early modern Turkic name (Barčuq / Barchuk) for the oasis later known as Maralbexi (Bachu).
b_barchuk.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym Barčuq (Barchuk), the pre-Qing name of Maralbexi (Chinese Bachu) on the lower Kashgar–Yarkand River plain, without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu, recording events of 169 CE) and Weilue (3rd century CE) as Zhenzhong, near modern Maralbashi.
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era fortified town in the Maralbashi/Barchuk oasis area.

b_tumshuk.first_mention_attestation: Modern Uyghur name Tumshuq ('beak/snout/promontory'), recorded in early 20th-century CE archaeological expeditions (Paul Pelliot, 1906–1909 CE) for the Toqquz-Sarai Buddhist ruins.
b_tumshuk.etymology_analysis: Modern Uyghur toponym Tumshuq ('beak, promontory', Chinese Tumushuke), applied to the Toqquz-Sarai Buddhist monastic site that flourished in the 4th–7th centuries CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tang dynasty records (Xin Tangshu) naming Jushide as the Tang-era garrison/district corresponding to the Tumshuq oasis.
older_name_by_867.notes: Center of the Eastern Iranian Tumshuqese Saka language and Serindian Buddhist art (4th–7th centuries CE).

b_uch_TARIM.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Turkic lexicon of Mahmud al-Kashgari (Diwan Lughat al-Turk, 1072–1074 CE) as Uč (Üch), later expanded to Uch-Turfan (Uqturpan).
b_uch_TARIM.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym Uč / Üč (later Uch-Turfan / Uqturpan), first attested in Mahmud al-Kashgari's 11th-century CE Diwan Lughat al-Turk.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Hanshu, 1st century BCE–1st century CE) and Hou Hanshu as Wensu, and Tang Annals (717 CE Battle of Aksu) for the oasis.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient oasis state of Wensu west of Aksu on the northern Silk Road.

b_stwerap.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE or medieval written attestation found; obscure/unverified toponym assigned to the Aksu region.

morphemes.translation: unattested settlement name in the Aksu region

b_stwerap.etymology_analysis: Unverified toponym in the Aksu region with no documented pre-867 CE written attestation or established etymology.

b_besinada.first_mention_attestation: Cartographic form 'Besinada' attested on 17th–18th century European maps (Nicolas Sanson 1648/1682; Guillaume Delisle 1706), representing the Circassian Principality of Besleney (formed in the 1530s CE) or the Balkar Basiane.
b_besinada.etymology_analysis: European cartographic rendering of the Circassian Principality of Besleney (Adyghe Besleney) or the neighboring Balkar Basiane.

b_majar.first_mention_attestation: Golden Horde city on the Kuma River attested by its own coinage in 1310–1311 CE and visited by Ibn Battuta around 1332 CE as al-Machar.
b_majar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Golden Horde trade city whose name derives from the Magyar autonym, linked to Hungarian/Eastern Magyar traditions in the North Caucasus.

b_cabarda.first_mention_attestation: Kabards and Kabardia first recorded in 15th-century sources (Giosafat Barbaro's 1436 Caucasus travels; Kabardia emerged as a political community in the 15th century CE), with an earlier Sea of Azov settlement Kobardi marked on Angelino Dulcert's 1339 CE map.
b_cabarda.etymology_analysis: From Kabardian Qabardey (Eastern Circassia), variously derived from the Kabar ethnonym, a legendary leader Qabard Tambiy, or Georgian/Nakh geographical terms.

b_tatartopa.first_mention_attestation: Golden Horde outpost known as Upper Dzhulat / Tatar-Tup attested in 14th-century North Caucasus and Timurid-era accounts (1361–1362 CE and 1395 CE); an earlier Alanic settlement existed from the 10th century CE (identified with 1277–1278 CE Dedyakov).
b_tatartopa.etymology_analysis: Ossetian Tætærtupp / Turkic Tatar-Tup ('Tatar camp/hill'), applied to the Golden Horde city of Upper Dzhulat on the left bank of the Terek River.

b_petigoria.first_mention_attestation: Historical region of Pyatigorye (Petigoria) in the North Caucasus attested from the late 15th to 16th century CE in Muscovite diplomatic records (e.g., 1492 CE Great Horde–Circassian conflict) and European maps.
b_petigoria.etymology_analysis: Russian calque of Turkic Beshtau ('five mountains'), denoting the historical North Caucasian region around Mount Beshtau.

b_maghas.first_mention_attestation: Capital of medieval Alania first attested in Islamic geographical literature by al-Mas'udi in Muruj al-Dhahab (940s CE, c. 943 CE) as Maghas / Ma'as.

morphemes.translation: capital city of Alania (exact Alanic root uncertain)

b_maghas.etymology_analysis: Recorded in Arabic as Maghas/Ma'as and in Persian as Magas/Makas; later medieval writers played on the Persian homonym magas ('fly').

b_etzeri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written records by 867 CE; Etseri is a historical community in Upper Svaneti, Georgia, whose surviving medieval stone churches (such as Pkhutreri) date to the 10th–11th centuries CE.
b_etzeri.etymology_analysis: Georgian/Svan toponym etseri, denoting a clearing or fern-covered alpine meadow in Upper Svaneti.

b_betzini.first_mention_attestation: Exact founding date unattested in written sources; archaeological evidence indicates permanent settlement in the Bezengi (Byzyngy) high-mountain valley of Kabardino-Balkaria from the Late Middle Ages.
b_betzini.etymology_analysis: From Karachay-Balkar Byzyngy, explained as buz ynngan ('place where the ice melted'), naming the high-mountain valley and glacier.

b_bata.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Greek colony and port of Bata (Greek: Βατά) on Tsemes Bay (modern Novorossiysk), attested in Strabo's Geographica (XI.2.14, c. 20 CE) and Ptolemy's Geographia (V.9.8, c. 150 CE).
b_bata.etymology_analysis: Classical Greek rendering (Βατά) of a pre-existing Maeotian/Sindian coastal settlement name on Tsemes Bay.

b_zapaxi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in documented historical sources before or after 867 CE; appears as a holding name in the historical-map tradition for Zichia without confirmed pre-867 written attestation.
b_zapaxi.etymology_analysis: Unattested holding name in Zichia with no confirmed etymology or written historical record.

b_ulmi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in documented historical sources before or after 867 CE; appears as a holding name in Zichia without confirmed pre-867 written attestation.
b_ulmi.etymology_analysis: Unattested holding name in Zichia with no confirmed etymology or written historical record.

b_ak-dzulpas.first_mention_attestation: Coastal site Akdzhulpas (Ak-Dzhulpas) on Saryshyganak Bay of the northern Aral Sea, first documented in June 1848 CE during Alexey Butakov's Aral Sea expedition (noted by Taras Shevchenko) and later by Nikolai Severtsov.
b_ak-dzulpas.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym from aq ('white') and local coastal/sacred tract name Dzhulpas on Saryshyganak Bay.

b_agypse.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Agyspe is a modern locality and Oligocene–Miocene fossil site in the Northern Aral region documented in 20th-century Soviet geological literature.
b_agypse.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym in the Northern Aral region, from aq ('white') and espe/yspe ('spring/seepage').

b_zhelanash.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Zhalanash is a modern former fishing village on the Aral Sea in Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan.
b_zhelanash.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh zhalaŋaš ('bare/naked'), describing an exposed, treeless shoreline on the Aral Sea.

b_kassarma.first_mention_attestation: Tract and freshwater springs of Kassarma along the Eastern Chink of the Ustyurt Plateau on the Aral Sea coast, attested in 1873 CE Russian military expedition accounts (E. S. Saranchev, 1874 CE).
b_kassarma.etymology_analysis: Local Karakalpak/Kazakh geographical name for a terrace and freshwater spring complex beneath the Eastern Chink of Ustyurt.

b_kulandy.first_mention_attestation: Kulandy Peninsula on the northern Aral Sea charted in July 1849 CE during Alexey Butakov's Aral Sea descriptive expedition; modern fishing village in Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan.
b_kulandy.etymology_analysis: Kazakh Qulandy ('abounding in kulans/wild asses'), naming the peninsula on the northern Aral Sea.

b_kugaral.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Kokaral (older spelling Kugaral) was an island in the northern Aral Sea (connected to the mainland from the 1960s–1973 CE).
b_kugaral.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Kökaral ('Green Island'), referring to the former island in the northern Aral Sea.

b_davlet-girei.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; local name Davlet-Girei applied in the 18th–19th centuries CE to the ruined fortress of Kurgancha-kala on the Ustyurt Plateau.
b_davlet-girei.eponym_details: Named in 18th–19th century CE local Karakalpak and Kazakh tradition after a figure bearing the post-867 Turco-Mongol dynastic name Davlet-Girei (Devlet Giray), applied to the ruins of Kurgancha-kala.
b_davlet-girei.etymology_analysis: Personal dynastic name Davlet-Girei (Devlet Giray), attached in local tradition to the Ustyurt fortress ruins.

b_kara-mugai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before or after 867 CE; minor Kazakh steppe toponym in the Aral region.
b_kara-mugai.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound toponym with qara ('black') and local element mugai.

b_tailyak-kul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before or after 867 CE; minor Kazakh lake toponym in the Aral region.

b_raimskoe.first_mention_attestation: Russian military outpost Fort Raim (Raimskoe) established in 1847 CE at the mouth of the Syr Darya around the ruined mausoleum of 18th-century Kazakh warrior Raiymbek Batyr.
b_raimskoe.eponym_details: Named after the 18th-century Kazakh warrior Raiymbek Batyr (1705–1785 CE), around whose ruined mausoleum the Russian fort was constructed in 1847 CE.
b_raimskoe.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival form Raimskoe derived from Fort Raim, itself named for the nearby mausoleum of Raiymbek Batyr.

b_dzangent.first_mention_attestation: The Kipchak/Russian form Jankent (Dzhankent) was first recorded by Russian army topographers in the early 19th century CE (visited by P. Lerkh in 1867 CE); it represents the same site as 10th-century CE Yangikent.
b_dzangent.etymology_analysis: Kipchak/Kazakh phonetic variant (Zhankent/Dzhankent) of Turkic Yangikent ('New Town').

b_yangikent.first_mention_attestation: Capital of the Oghuz Yabgu State on the lower Syr Darya, first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (Ibn Rusta, c. 903–913 CE; al-Mas'udi, 940s CE) as Jengi-Kent / al-Qaryat al-Haditha.
b_yangikent.etymology_analysis: Oghuz Turkic Yangikent ('New Town'), translated into Arabic as al-Qaryat al-Haditha and Persian as Dih-i Naw.

b_kazalinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1853 CE as Russian Fort No. 1 on the right bank of the Syr Darya, and granted town status under the name Kazalinsk in 1867 CE.
b_kazalinsk.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of Kazakh Qazaly (Kazaly), denoting a traditional fishing-weir/reed-trap site on the Syr Darya.

b_buzai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before or after 867 CE; minor Kazakh steppe toponym in the lower Syr Darya / Aral region.
b_buzai.etymology_analysis: Minor Kazakh toponym in the Aral region with no pre-867 written attestation.

b_koskul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Koskul is a descriptive Kazakh lake toponym in the Aral / Syr Darya basin.
b_koskul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym Qosköl ('Twin/Double Lake'), referring to paired steppe lakes.

b_atyrau.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1640–1645 CE as a Russian wooden fort (Yaitskiy Gorodok / Guryev) at the mouth of the Ural (Yaik) River; renamed Atyrau in 1991 CE from the Kazakh geographic term for the delta.
b_atyrau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh geographical term atyrau ('river delta/estuary'), traditionally applied to the branched mouth of the Ural River on the Caspian Sea.

b_taisugan.first_mention_attestation: Taisugan Sands and locality in Atyrau Region, Kazakhstan, attested in late 18th-century CE Kazakh historical records (birthplace of Isatay Taymanuly in 1791 CE); unattested before 867 CE.
b_taisugan.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Taysoyğan ('where a foal was slaughtered'), naming the sand-dune massif and village in Atyrau Region.

b_hyan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before or after 867 CE; minor steppe toponym in Atyrau Region.
b_hyan.etymology_analysis: Unattested minor toponym in the Atyrau steppe with no confirmed pre-867 written record.

b_bakash-aul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Kazakh compound toponym denoting an aul (encampment/village) in Atyrau Region.
b_bakash-aul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh settlement name combining Bakash with aul ('encampment/village').

b_baisary.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Baisary is a ridge and winter camp (kystau) near Southern Ustyurt / Mugalzhar in western Kazakhstan.
b_baisary.etymology_analysis: Kazakh toponym Baysary, naming a ridge and winter pasture area in western Kazakhstan.

b_sorkul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Sorkul is a descriptive Kazakh salt-lake toponym in Atyrau Region.
b_sorkul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym Sorköl ('Salt-pan Lake'), denoting a saline lake in the Caspian/Uil basin.

b_tulugai_sor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Kazakh salt-marsh (sor) toponym in Atyrau Region.
b_tulugai_sor.etymology_analysis: Kazakh topographic name combining Tulugai with sor ('salt marsh/alkali flat').

b_kainar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Kainar is a well, river, and 18th–20th century CE religious-residential complex in Zhylyoi District, Atyrau Region.
b_kainar.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh qaynar ('spring/source'), naming a well and river in Atyrau Region.

b_zarapan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before or after 867 CE; minor steppe toponym in Atyrau Region.
b_zarapan.etymology_analysis: Unattested minor toponym in Atyrau Region with no confirmed pre-867 written record.

b_sagiz.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Sagiz (Saghyz) is a 511 km steppe river in Aktobe and Atyrau regions, Kazakhstan.
b_sagiz.etymology_analysis: Ancient western Kazakhstani hydronym Sağyz (Sagiz), interpreted as 'marshy/clay-banked river' with an archaic -yz/-uz ('river') suffix.

b_ulu-uil.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Ulu-Uil is the older Russian/Kazakh rendering of the Uil (Oiyl) River in western Kazakhstan.
b_ulu-uil.etymology_analysis: Older form Ulu-Uil ('Great Uil') distinguishing the main 800 km Uil (Oiyl) River from its tributaries.

b_jarkul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before 867 CE; Jarkul is a descriptive Kazakh lake toponym in western Kazakhstan.

b_bekdas.first_mention_attestation: Soviet coastal settlement on Bekdas Bay of the Caspian Sea in Turkmenistan, granted worker's settlement status in 1963 CE and renamed Garabogaz in 2002 CE.
b_bekdas.etymology_analysis: Turkmen Bekdaş ('firm stone'), naming the Caspian coastal cape, bay, and 20th-century chemical-port settlement.

b_sumbe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources before or after 867 CE; minor toponym in the Ustyurt–Garabogazkol borderland.
b_sumbe.etymology_analysis: Minor Turkmen/Kazakh borderland toponym with no confirmed pre-867 written attestation.

b_kyzyl-su.first_mention_attestation: Russian expedition of Alexander Bekovich-Cherkassky landed and built a fortified settlement near Kyzyl-Su in 1717 CE; permanent Russian fort Krasnovodsk was established in 1869 CE (translating Turkmen Kyzyl-Su, 'Red Water').
b_kyzyl-su.etymology_analysis: Turkmen/Oghuz compound from gyzyl ('red') and suw ('water'), referring to the reddish coastal waters of the bay; later calqued into Russian as Krasnovodsk in 1869 CE and renamed Türkmenbaşy in 1993 CE.

b_yangadzha.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; modern village and military airfield (now Ýaňyajy) in Türkmenbaşy District, Balkan Province, Turkmenistan.
b_yangadzha.etymology_analysis: Turkmen toponym (modern Ýaňyajy, Russian Yangadzha) likely combining ýaňy ('new') and ajy ('bitter, brackish'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_oglamych.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; modern village (now Awlamyş) in Türkmenbaşy District, Balkan Province, Turkmenistan.
b_oglamych.etymology_analysis: From Turkmen awlamyş, the past participle of awlamak ('to hunt'), meaning 'hunted'; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_kum-sebszen.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; sandy desert tract (Kumsebshen) between the Tuarkyr and Kaplankyr uplands in northwestern Turkmenistan.
b_kum-sebszen.etymology_analysis: Turkmen physical-geographic name for the northern part of the Uchtagankum sandy desert (Kumsebshen), from kum ('sand') and a derivative of sepmek ('to scatter, strew').

b_itil.first_mention_attestation: Established c. 750 CE as the capital of the Khazar Khaganate in the Volga Delta; the Turkic hydronym Yitil/Itil is attested in Ibn Khordadbeh (9th century CE) and the city name Atil/Itil in 10th-century CE Arabic sources (earlier 9th-century CE sources also refer to the Khazar capital as Khamlij).
b_itil.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym (Atil/Itil, literally 'great river') denoting the Volga River, attested as Yitil/Itil in Ibn Khordadbeh (9th century CE) and adopted for the Khazar Khaganate's Volga Delta capital (established c. 750 CE; 9th-century Arabic sources also call the capital Khamlij/Hamlikh, recorded on b_astrakhan, while the twin-city name Khazaran appears in 10th-century CE sources).

b_saray.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1242 CE by Batu Khan as the capital of the Golden Horde (Sarai Batu / Old Sarai) on the lower Volga.
b_saray.etymology_analysis: From Persian sarāy ('palace, court'); founded in the 1240s CE by Batu Khan as the Golden Horde capital (often distinguished as Sarai Batu, though the barony title itself is Saray).

b_nikolaievsk.first_mention_attestation: 1794 CE (Nikolaevskaya Sloboda named; originally settled in 1747 CE as Dmitriyev).
b_nikolaievsk.etymology_analysis: Russian town name derived from Nikolay (Saint Nicholas, reflected in the 1794 CE sloboda name Nikolayevskaya) with the toponymic suffix -evsk.

b_chyorny_yar.first_mention_attestation: Established as a Russian military fort on the left bank of the Volga in 1627 CE (moved to the right bank seven years later).
b_chyorny_yar.etymology_analysis: Russian topographic name meaning 'black bluff' (chyorny 'black' + yar 'steep bank/bluff', a borrowing from Turkic yar).

b_saqsin.first_mention_attestation: Medieval city in the Volga Delta flourishing from the 11th to 13th centuries CE, first attested in 11th–12th century CE Islamic geographical sources (e.g., al-Gharnati).
b_saqsin.etymology_analysis: Medieval Volga Delta city (11th–13th centuries CE); scholars propose Saqsin is an Arabized form of Turkic Saryghsin ('Yellow/White City'), possibly succeeding nearby Atil after its fall.

b_saraychiq.first_mention_attestation: Medieval city on the lower Ural River flourishing between the 10th and 16th centuries CE (attested in medieval Perso-Arabic and Turkic sources as Sarāyjūq / Sarayçık).
b_saraychiq.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Persian-Turkic name meaning 'Little Sarai' or 'Little Palace' (Persian sarāy + Turkic diminutive -čyq/-shyq).

b_ryn.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; desert region (Ryn-Peski / Naryn-Qūmy) between the lower Volga and Ural rivers.

morphemes.translation: narrow, fine (shortened in Russian to Ryn)

b_ryn.etymology_analysis: Russian shortened form of Kazakh Naryn-Qūmy ('Naryn Sands'), from Mongolic/Turkic nariin ('narrow, fine').

b_ukek.first_mention_attestation: Golden Horde city on the Volga near modern Saratov, founded c. 1240–1250 CE and attested in 13th–14th century CE sources (including Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta).
b_ukek.etymology_analysis: From Turkic ükäk ('tower, fortification, chest/coffer'), referring to the fortified Golden Horde river port founded in the mid-13th century CE.

b_engels.first_mention_attestation: 1931 CE (renamed Engels after Friedrich Engels; originally founded in 1747 CE as Pokrovskaya Sloboda).
b_engels.eponym_details: Renamed Engels in 1931 CE after German socialist philosopher Friedrich Engels (1820–1895 CE).
b_engels.etymology_analysis: Modern Soviet renaming (1931 CE) of Pokrovsk/Kosakenstadt in honor of Friedrich Engels (1820–1895 CE).

b_uzen.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Turkic hydronym for the Bolshoy and Maly Uzen rivers (modern town of Novouzensk was founded in 1760 CE).
b_uzen.etymology_analysis: From Turkic/Kazakh özen ('river, stream'), Russianized as Uzen for the Bolshoy and Maly Uzen steppe rivers.

b_verchina_uzen.first_mention_attestation: Village of Verkhny Uzen in Yershovsky District, Saratov Oblast, on the Bolshoy Uzen River; officially founded in 1780 CE.
b_verchina_uzen.etymology_analysis: Russian-Turkic settlement locator meaning 'Upper Uzen' (verkhny 'upper' + Uzen from Turkic özen 'river'), founded in 1780 CE on the upper Bolshoy Uzen.

b_chelykla.first_mention_attestation: Chalykla railway settlement in Ozinsky District, Saratov Oblast, attested by 1900 CE (birthplace of Ivan Maslennikov); named after the Chalykla River, with no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_chelykla.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bolshaya/Malaya Chalykla River, from a Turkic hydronymic stem meaning 'reedy/brushwood place'.

b_akkityk.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym in western Kazakhstan.
b_akkityk.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym beginning with aq ('white, clear'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_issenjau.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym in western Kazakhstan.
b_issenjau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic compound toponym (compare personal/clan name Esen-zhau); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_churuk.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; medieval Silk Road caravanserai/station (Shuruk) on the Mangystau/Ustyurt route in western Kazakhstan.
b_churuk.etymology_analysis: Turkic steppe toponym (Shuruk/Churuk) associated with a medieval Silk Road caravanserai on the Ustyurt/Mangystau route; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_sam.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Sam Sands (Peski Sam) sandy desert massif on the Ustyurt Plateau in western Kazakhstan.

morphemes.translation: sandy tract / steppe toponym of uncertain origin

b_sam.etymology_analysis: Name of the Sam Sands desert massif on the Ustyurt Plateau; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_kos-buwak.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kosbulak (Qosbulaq) spring, solonchak, and geological trough in the North Ustyurt Basin, western Kazakhstan.
b_kos-buwak.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Qosbulaq ('twin springs'), combining qos ('pair, twin') and bulaq ('spring'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_chumishtikul.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Shomyshtykol (Shumyshtykol) salt lake/depression in western Kazakhstan.
b_chumishtikul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym (Shömishtiköl) meaning 'ladle-shaped lake', from shömishti ('ladle-shaped') and köl ('lake'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_namastau.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic toponym in western Kazakhstan.
b_namastau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh-Persian compound toponym from namaz ('prayer') and tau ('mountain'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_kashkarata.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Koshkar-Ata lake and necropolis in Mangystau Region date from the 10th–19th centuries CE.
b_kashkarata.eponym_details: Named after the Sufi saint Koshkar-Ata (Khoja Koshkar-Ata), whose Mangystau necropolis and cultic tradition date to the 10th–19th centuries CE (post-867 CE).
b_kashkarata.etymology_analysis: Named after the legendary Sufi saint Koshkar-Ata (Kazakh qoshqar 'ram' + ata 'father/saint'), whose Mangystau necropolis dates to the 10th–19th centuries CE.

b_asheh-atrik.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym in western Kazakhstan.
b_asheh-atrik.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym containing ashchy ('bitter, salty'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_qoshagyl.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; modern village and hydrocarbon locality (Koshagyl) in Zhylyoi District, Atyrau Region, Kazakhstan.
b_qoshagyl.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound from qos ('pair, double') and aghyl ('corral, sheepfold'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_azgyl.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; village of Azghyr (Azgir) in Kurmangazy District, Atyrau Region, Kazakhstan.
b_azgyl.etymology_analysis: Kazakh steppe toponym (Azghyr/Azgir) in Atyrau Region; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_kumstan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Turkic-Persian steppe toponym in western Kazakhstan.
b_kumstan.etymology_analysis: Turkic-Persian compound meaning 'sandy land', from qum ('sand') and -stan ('land, place of'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_tengiz.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented for the locality; the Tengiz oil field and settlement in Zhylyoi District, Atyrau Region, were discovered/established in 1979 CE.
b_tengiz.etymology_analysis: From Turco-Mongol tengiz / Kazakh teñiz ('sea'), referring to the northeastern Caspian coast.

b_beyneu.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; village of Beyneu in Mangystau Region expanded into a town in the 1970s CE following oil discovery.
b_beyneu.etymology_analysis: Kazakh steppe toponym (Beineu) in Mangystau Region; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_kajdak.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kaydak Inlet (Sor Kaydak) is a saline inlet of the Caspian Sea bordering the Buzachi Peninsula.

morphemes.translation: saline inlet toponym of uncertain etymology

b_kajdak.etymology_analysis: Name of the Kaydak Inlet (Sor Kaydak) off the northeastern Caspian Sea; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_koizak.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym on the Buzachi Peninsula.
b_koizak.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym on the Buzachi Peninsula, likely containing qoy ('sheep'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_aktau.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1958 CE as a uranium-mining settlement (Melovoye / Guryev-20), granted town status and named Aktau in 1963 CE (Shevchenko 1964–1991 CE, then restored as Aktau).
b_aktau.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh Aqtau ('White Mountain'), referring to the white chalk cliffs along the Caspian coast; the city itself was founded in 1958 CE.

b_karasye.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Russian-adapted toponym (Karasye) in the Mangystau area.
b_karasye.etymology_analysis: Russian toponymic form from karas ('crucian carp') or Russianized adaptation of a local Turkic name; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_fort_aleksandrovkiy.first_mention_attestation: 1857 CE (renamed Fort-Aleksandrovsky after Tsar Alexander II; originally founded in 1846 CE as Novopetrovskoye).
b_fort_aleksandrovkiy.eponym_details: Renamed Fort-Aleksandrovskii in 1857 CE after Russian Emperor Alexander II (1818–1881 CE).
b_fort_aleksandrovkiy.etymology_analysis: Russian imperial fort name ('Alexander's Fort') adopted in 1857 CE for the 1846 CE Novopetrovskoye fortress on Cape Tyub-Karagan.

b_porsu-burun.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Cape Porsu (Porsu-Burun) on the Caspian coast of the Mangyshlak Peninsula.
b_porsu-burun.etymology_analysis: Turkic coastal cape name combining porsu ('badger' or 'stagnant/sulfurous') and burun ('nose, cape, promontory'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_fort_novoaleksandrovkiy.first_mention_attestation: Russian military fortification Novo-Aleksandrovskoye (New Alexander Fort) built in 1834 CE on the southern coast of Dead Kultuk / Kaydak Bay (abandoned in 1846 CE).
b_fort_novoaleksandrovkiy.eponym_details: Named Novo-Aleksandrovskoye in 1834 CE after Russian Emperor Alexander I (1777–1825 CE) or Tsarevich Alexander (later Alexander II, 1818–1881 CE).
b_fort_novoaleksandrovkiy.etymology_analysis: Russian colonial fort name ('New Alexander Fort') built in 1834 CE on Kaydak Bay; the game repo's indigenous restitution label Mangystau is a regional peninsula name, not a pre-867 CE written attestation of this fort.

b_busaga.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic toponym (Bosaga) on the Mangystau/Ustyurt plateau.
b_busaga.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh bosagha ('threshold, doorway'), used geographically for a pass or escarpment threshold; no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_bailjar.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic steppe toponym on the Ustyurt plateau.
b_bailjar.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic pluralized clan or settlement toponym (Baylar, 'the rich/nobles'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_sai-kule.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation documented; Kazakh/Turkic hydronymic toponym on the Ustyurt plateau.
b_sai-kule.etymology_analysis: Kazakh/Turkic compound from say ('gully, ravine') and köl ('lake'); no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_chah.first_mention_attestation: Sasanian Middle Persian inscription of Shapur I at Ka'ba-ye Zartosht (262 CE) as Cac, and 5th-7th century CE Chinese chronicles (Book of Sui, Old Book of Tang) and Xuanzang (629 CE) as Zheshi/Shi.

morphemes.translation: oasis-region name (possibly from Old Iranian *caica- 'water/lake' or *kank- 'stone')

b_chah.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Iranian toponym (Sogdian/Middle Persian Cac, Arabized as al-Shash), attested in Shapur I's 262 CE Res Gestae and Chinese chronicles as Zheshi/Shi ('stone'). Later adapted in Turkic as Tashkent ('stone city').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Chinese Han-era historical chronicles (2nd century BCE) recording Beitian (Pi-tien) as the summer capital of Kangju in the Tashkent oasis.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Kangju summer capital in the Chirchik/Tashkent oasis preceding the medieval urban center of Chach/Binkat.

b_sayram.first_mention_attestation: Mahmud al-Kashgari's Diwan Lughat al-Turk (1072-1074 CE), which records Sayram as an alternate name for Isfijab alongside the river name seyrem suw ('shallow water').
b_sayram.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronymic toponym (Sayram), linked by Mahmud al-Kashgari (11th century CE) to seyrem suw ('shallow water'), the name of the river running east of the town. The site was earlier known as Isfijab (audited separately as b_isfijab).

b_chimkent.first_mention_attestation: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi's Zafar-nama (completed 1425 CE), recording Chimkent during Timur's military campaigns of 1365-1366 CE; archaeological layers date from the 11th-12th century CE.
b_chimkent.etymology_analysis: Turco-Iranian compound meaning 'turf town' or 'green/sodded city' (Turkic chim/shym 'turf, sod' + Sogdian/Iranian kent 'town'), first attested in writing in early 15th-century Timurid historiography.

b_nuket.first_mention_attestation: Mid-8th century CE coinage of Chach issued at Nudjket (c. 750 CE) bearing the legend of sovereign Nanchu (Banchu) Ertegin, and later in 10th-12th century CE Islamic geographies (al-Idrisi, Ibn Hawqal) as Nukath/Nujkath.
b_nuket.etymology_analysis: Sogdian/Iranian compound toponym (Nujkath/Nukath, 'New Town'), attested on mid-8th century CE Chach coinage and later as a major town and capital of Ilak in medieval Islamic geographies.

b_isfijab.first_mention_attestation: 9th-century CE Islamic historical and geographical sources recording the Samanid conquest of Isfijab by Nuh ibn Asad in 840 CE (and subsequent mentions in Ibn Khordadbeh and al-Tabari).
b_isfijab.etymology_analysis: Iranian toponym (Isfijab/Ispidjab), glossed by Mahmud al-Kashgari as 'White City' (from Sogdian/Persian ispid/sipid 'white'), attested as the chief frontier city of the middle Syr Darya oasis by 840 CE.

b_otrar.first_mention_attestation: Karakhanid-era sources (11th-12th century CE), when the name Otrar gradually superseded the earlier Islamic name Farab/Parab.

morphemes.translation: medieval oasis-city name on the middle Syr Darya

b_otrar.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym first attested in the Karakhanid period (11th century CE), replacing the earlier Perso-Arabic name Farab and Old Turkic Kengu Tarman.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Turkic Orkhon inscriptions (Kul Tigin, 732 CE) for Kengu Tarman, and 9th-10th century CE Islamic geographies (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi) for Farab/Parab.
older_name_by_867.notes: Pre-Karakhanid names of the Otrar oasis center before the toponym Otrar became predominant in the 11th-13th centuries CE.

b_chakpak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern Kazakh toponym (Chakpak / Shaqpaq Pass and settlement) recorded in 19th-20th century CE geographical surveys.
b_chakpak.etymology_analysis: Kazakh topographic name derived from shaqpaq ('flint, strike-stone'), referring to the Chakpak mountain pass between the Talas and Arys basins.

b_awliya-ata.first_mention_attestation: Kokand-era renaming in 1856 CE of the settlement built on the ruins of Taraz (previously Namangan-i Kochek) to Aulie-Ata ('Holy Father').
b_awliya-ata.eponym_details: Named in 1856 CE after 'Awliya-Ata' ('Holy Father'), the popular honorific title of the 10th-11th century CE Karakhanid ruler Qarakhan, whose mausoleum stands in the city.
b_awliya-ata.etymology_analysis: 19th-century CE Turco-Arabic honorific name ('Holy Father') applied in 1856 CE to the Kokand fortress town on the site of ancient Taraz/Talas, in honor of the Karakhanid ruler Qarakhan (the ancient/medieval predecessor Taraz/Talas is audited separately as b_talas).

b_shavgar.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works, notably Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), describing Shavgar as a major fortified town in the Turkestan oasis.
b_shavgar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Iranian/Sogdian toponym (Shavgar, Turkicized later as Qaračuq), attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies as the chief urban center of the Turkestan oasis prior to the rise of Yasi.

b_sawran.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Arab geographer al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), who described Sawran (Sabran) as a large city surrounded by seven walls with an inner-city mosque.

morphemes.translation: medieval fortified oasis-city on the middle Syr Darya

b_sawran.etymology_analysis: Medieval Syr Darya urban toponym (Sawran/Sabran), first attested in writing by al-Muqaddasi in the late 10th century CE, though the nearby precursor site of Qaratobe has archaeological layers from the 1st-6th centuries CE.

b_shulak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern Kazakh toponym (Shulak / Sholakkorgan) in the Turkistan region, documented in 19th-20th century CE records.
b_shulak.etymology_analysis: Modern Kazakh toponym derived from sholaq ('short, truncated'), associated with Sholakkorgan in the northern Karatau foothills.

b_yasi.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century CE Islamic and Sufi hagiographical sources associated with Khoja Ahmad Yasawi (1093-1166 CE), who settled and died in Yasi.
b_yasi.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym (Yasy/Yesi, 'flat, broad'), which rose to prominence in the 12th century CE as the seat of Khoja Ahmad Yasawi and later became known as Hazrat-i Turkistan.

b_sutkend.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works, first in Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE), describing Sutkend as a riverside town west of Shash where Muslim Turks gathered.
b_sutkend.etymology_analysis: Turco-Iranian hybrid toponym meaning 'Milk Town' (Turkic sut 'milk' + Sogdian/Iranian kent 'town'), attested in 10th-century CE Arabic and Persian geographical texts.

b_akkum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern Kazakh geographic and settlement name in the Syr Darya basin.
b_akkum.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh descriptive topographic name meaning 'White Sand' (aq 'white' + qum 'sand'), common across sandy tracts of the Syr Darya and Aralkum region.

b_sary-ozek.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern Kazakh toponym recorded in 19th-20th century CE geographical surveys.
b_sary-ozek.etymology_analysis: Kazakh topographic compound meaning 'Yellow Valley' or 'Yellow Channel' (sary 'yellow' + ozek 'valley, dry streambed').

b_mushun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; local steppe toponym in the Muyunkum region.
b_mushun.etymology_analysis: Unattested local toponym of uncertain etymology used for a steppe locality in the Muyunkum desert-steppe zone.

b_karakul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; modern Turkic/Kazakh hydronymic toponym in the Muyunkum region.
b_karakul.etymology_analysis: Standard Turkic hydronym meaning 'Black Lake' (qara 'black' + kol 'lake'), widespread across Central Asia.

b_quriltay.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE Mongol-era chronicles (Secret History of the Mongols, c. 1240 CE; later associated with the 1269 CE Kurultai of Talas), introducing the political-assembly term into Central Asia.
b_quriltay.etymology_analysis: Mongolic/Turkic political term meaning 'assembly' or 'council' (from khural/qur- 'to gather'), anachronistic as a settlement name prior to the 13th-century CE Mongol period.

b_talas.first_mention_attestation: Byzantine historian Menander Protector (568 CE), recording the embassy of Zemarchus to the Western Turkic Khaganate at Talas, followed by Xuanzang (629 CE) and accounts of the Battle of Talas (751 CE).

morphemes.translation: river and valley name in southern Kazakhstan and northwestern Kyrgyzstan

b_talas.etymology_analysis: Ancient hydronym and valley name (Talas), attested in Byzantine (568 CE), Chinese (629 CE), and early Islamic (751 CE) sources.

b_shelji.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Arab geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), describing Shelji (Shalji) as a mountain town and silver-mining center near Talas.

morphemes.translation: medieval silver-mining town in the Talas mountains

b_shelji.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym of a prominent silver-mining town in the Talas valley, first documented in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical literature.

b_symbyl.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern local toponym in the Talas-Muyunkum region.
b_symbyl.etymology_analysis: Modern/unattested local toponym in the Talas-Muyunkum borderland, possibly reflecting Perso-Turkic sumbul ('hyacinth, spikenard').

b_itte-kichu.first_mention_attestation: 19th-century CE geographical accounts of the Kazakh steppe, notably Shoqan Walikhanov's Ocherki Dzhungarii (c. 1860 CE), which cites the meridian of It-Kechu on the Chu/Talas steppe.
b_itte-kichu.etymology_analysis: Turkic topographic compound meaning 'Dog's Ford' (it 'dog' + kechu 'ford, crossing'), documented in 19th-century CE steppe geography.

b_jend.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers, notably Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), mentioning Jand as an Oghuz Turkish town on the lower Syr Darya (later Seljuk Beg's seat c. 985 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval Oghuz town on the lower Syr Darya

b_jend.etymology_analysis: Medieval lower Syr Darya urban toponym (Jand/Jend), first attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geography as an Oghuz settlement and famous as the seat of the early Seljuk clan.

b_uzun-kul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; documented in 19th-early 20th century CE Russian geographical surveys (e.g., 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica) as an elongated lake group near the lower Syr Darya and Sarysu.
b_uzun-kul.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronym meaning 'Long Lake' (uzun 'long' + kol 'lake'), referring to the elongated lake system in the lower Syr Darya / Sarysu basin.

b_beljan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern local toponym in the lower Syr Darya region.
b_beljan.etymology_analysis: Unattested local Kazakh/Turkic toponym in the lower Syr Darya region, likely combining bel ('ridge, pass') with jan ('side' or anthroponymic element).

b_azez-kul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern Kazakh-Arabic hydronymic toponym in the lower Syr Darya basin.
b_azez-kul.etymology_analysis: Post-Islamization Arabo-Turkic hydronym meaning 'Sacred/Dear Lake' (Arabic aziz 'revered, dear' + Turkic kol 'lake').

b_sighnaq.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works, notably Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), describing Sighnaq as a town on the Syr Darya (later Kipchak and Kazakh Khanate capital).
b_sighnaq.etymology_analysis: Turkic toponym meaning 'shelter' or 'refuge', first attested in late 10th-century CE Islamic geographical literature.

b_aq-masjid.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1817 CE (or 1820 CE) as the Kokand fortress of Ak-Mechet ('White Mosque'), later renamed Fort Perovsk (1853 CE) and Kyzylorda (1925 CE).
b_aq-masjid.etymology_analysis: 19th-century CE Turco-Arabic fortress name meaning 'White Mosque' (Turkic aq 'white' + Arabic masjid 'mosque'), founded by the Khanate of Kokand in 1817 CE.

b_tashti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern Kazakh toponym (Tasty) in the Syr Darya / Kyzylorda region.
b_tashti.etymology_analysis: Turkic/Kazakh topographic adjective meaning 'stony' (tash 'stone' + -ty adjectival suffix), designating a stony locality.

b_suzak.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE historical documents as Khuzak (archaeological horizons date from the 10th-18th centuries CE), and 16th-century CE chronicles as Suzak (capital of the Kazakh Khanate c. 1465-1469 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval fortified town north of the Karatau range

b_suzak.etymology_analysis: Medieval town name (attested as Khuzak in the 13th century CE and Suzak/Sozaq by the 15th-16th centuries CE), with archaeological occupation beginning around the 10th century CE.

b_uzgend_KARA.first_mention_attestation: 15th-century CE Timurid and Shaybanid chronicles (recording Muhammad Shaybani's capture of Syghnaq, Arkuk, and Uzgend on the Syr Darya in 1485 CE); archaeological remains of Ozgent date to the 12th-17th centuries CE.
b_uzgend_KARA.etymology_analysis: Turco-Iranian settlement name (Uzgend/Ozgent on the lower Syr Darya near Zhanakorgan, distinct from Uzgen in Fergana), paired with qara ('black/great') in the title key.

b_telegul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval written sources; modern Kazakh hydronym (Telikol) in the Syr Darya and Shieli districts of Kyzylorda Region.
b_telegul.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym (Telikol, rendered Telegul) referring to the shallow, reed-lined lake basin between the Daryalyk Takyr plain and Ashchykol depression in Kyzylorda Region.

b_oktyabr.first_mention_attestation: 20th-century CE Soviet-era settlement and kolkhoz name in Kyzylorda Region (e.g., Oktyabr kolkhoz, 1957-1972 CE), named after the October Revolution of 1917 CE.
b_oktyabr.etymology_analysis: 20th-century CE Soviet ideological settlement name derived from Russian Oktyabr ('October'), commemorating the October Revolution of 1917 CE.

b_badakhshan.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Chinese Buddhist pilgrim account of Xuanzang (629 CE, recorded in Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, 646 CE) as Po-to-chang-na, referring to a kingdom in the lower Kokcha basin.
b_badakhshan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Sasanian official title bēdaxš / badaxš (from Old Iranian *pati-axša, 'overseer') combined with the Iranian toponymic suffix -ān ('land of'), indicating a territory governed by or assigned to a badaxš.

b_rustaq.first_mention_attestation: Late 9th-century CE Arabic geographical work Kitab al-Buldan by al-Ya'qubi (891 CE), mentioning a local ruler of Rustabik (modern Rustaq) named al-Harith ibn Asad.
b_rustaq.etymology_analysis: From Persian rustāq (Middle Persian rōstāg), denoting a rural administrative district or agricultural sub-region.

b_kishm.first_mention_attestation: 8th-century CE historical narrative preserved in al-Tabari's Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk for the year 736 CE, recording a mosque at Kishm during the Umayyad pursuit of al-Harith ibn Surayj into Badakhshan.

morphemes.translation: settlement and valley toponym in western Badakhshan

b_kishm.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Eastern Iranian settlement name in the western Kokcha/Kishm basin of Badakhshan, attested in early Islamic conquest accounts by 736 CE.
