b_jerm.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; locally associated in later tradition with Timur (late 14th century CE) and documented in 19th-century CE gazetteers as Jurm/Jorm.
b_jerm.etymology_analysis: Settlement on the Kokcha River in Badakhshan; local folk etymology derives the name from Persian jurm ('fine/penalty'), allegedly imposed by Timur on the villagers in the late 14th century CE.

b_upper_karran.first_mention_attestation: The composite directional title 'Upper Karran' has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the underlying upper Kokcha valley of Kuran/Karran was noted by Xuanzang (629 CE) as Kiu-lang-na.

morphemes.translation: mountain valley district in southern Badakhshan

b_upper_karran.etymology_analysis: Modern/game-era directional subdivision ('Upper') applied to the historical mountain district of Karran/Kuran (Kiran wa Munjan) in the upper Kokcha valley.

b_lower_karran.first_mention_attestation: The composite directional title 'Lower Karran' (or standardized 'Nider-Karran') has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE, being a modern/game subdivision of the Karran/Kuran valley.

morphemes.translation: mountain valley district in southern Badakhshan

b_lower_karran.etymology_analysis: Modern/game-era directional subdivision ('Lower') applied to the lower reach of the historical Karran/Kuran valley in Badakhshan.

b_munjan.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Chinese Buddhist pilgrim account of Xuanzang (629 CE, recorded in Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, 646 CE) as Mengjian (Munjan), an old territory of Tukhara.

morphemes.translation: valley and ethnonym of the Munji people

b_munjan.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian regional and valley name (Munji/Persian Munjān, Chinese transcription Mengjian in 629 CE), associated with the Munji-speaking population of southern Badakhshan.

b_sanglich.first_mention_attestation: Late 10th-century CE Persian geography Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 26, 16) as S.nglnj (Sanglich), noted for its mountain garnet/ruby mines and hot spring.
b_sanglich.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym of the Sanglech valley in Badakhshan (related to Iranian sang, 'stone'), first attested in the 982 CE Hudud al-'Alam.

b_zaybak.first_mention_attestation: Early 11th-century CE works of al-Biruni (c. 1030 CE), where the Badakhshan locality of Zaybak/Zebak is attested.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (possibly linked to zaybaq, 'quicksilver', or local Pamiri root)

b_zaybak.etymology_analysis: Mountain settlement in eastern Badakhshan along the route to Ishkashim and Chitral; attested from the 11th century CE in al-Biruni.

b_shughnan.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Chinese Buddhist pilgrim account of Xuanzang (629 CE, recorded in 646 CE) as Shiqini, corroborated by the Old Tibetan Annals (756 CE, Shig nig) and al-Tabari (811-812 CE, Siqinan).
b_shughnan.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian regional name (Shughni Khughnān, Persian Shughnān), derived by Iranologists from an ethnonymic base related to the Saka (*Saka-nām / *Šiknān) with the plural/locative suffix -ān.

b_alichur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented as a high-altitude Pamir valley and Kyrgyz/Pamiri settlement only in 19th- and 20th-century CE records.
b_alichur.etymology_analysis: High-altitude Pamir settlement and valley name in Gorno-Badakhshan, popularly explained in local folklore as 'Ali's curse' due to its harsh, freezing winds.

b_murghab.first_mention_attestation: Late 19th-century CE Imperial Russian military records (1893 CE) establishing Pamirsky Post at the Bartang/Murghab river crossing, later renamed Murghab in the Soviet era.
b_murghab.etymology_analysis: Modern town founded in 1893 CE as Pamirsky Post and named after the Murghab River (Persian margh-āb 'prairie river' or murgh-āb 'bird river').

b_muji.first_mention_attestation: 20th-century CE Chinese administrative records (1962 CE, establishment of Muji Commune in Akto County, Xinjiang), named after the Muji mud volcanoes.
b_muji.etymology_analysis: From Kyrgyz, referring to the volcanic mudstone of the Muji crater group on the eastern Pamir Plateau, after which the modern township was named.

b_badakhshan_TARIM.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement; game-map unoccupied placeholder combining the regional names Badakhshan and Tarim.
b_badakhshan_TARIM.etymology_analysis: Synthetic game-map identifier for an unoccupied Pamir-Tarim borderland barony, not a historical settlement.

b_wakhan.first_mention_attestation: 1st-century CE Chinese Han chronicles (Book of Han / Book of Later Han, c. 1st century CE) as Xiumi, one of the five xihou principalities of the Yuezhi/Kushans, later Huomi in Tang sources and Wakhan in Islamic geography.
b_wakhan.etymology_analysis: Ancient Eastern Iranian regional name (Wakhi/Persian Wakhān, rendered in Han Chinese as Xiumi and Tang Chinese as Huomi), denoting the upper Oxus/Panj valley of the Wakhi people.

b_ishkamish.first_mention_attestation: Late 10th-century CE Persian geography Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 26, 14) as Sikashim (Ishkashim), described as the chief town of the region of Wakhan.
b_ishkamish.etymology_analysis: Proposed by Iranologist T. N. Pakhalina to derive from Indo-Iranian *sakā-kṣ̌amā ('land of the Saka'), attested in 982 CE as Sikāshim.

b_dar-i-tubbat.first_mention_attestation: Late 10th-century CE Persian geography Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 26, 12) as Dar-i Tubbat, a mountain-gate toll village on the approach to Wakhan.
b_dar-i-tubbat.etymology_analysis: Persian compound toponym meaning 'Gate of Tibet', denoting a fortified toll-gate village in Wakhan guarding the route toward Tibetan-held territory, first attested in 982 CE.

b_akhsikath.first_mention_attestation: Early 8th-century CE Arab conquest accounts of Fergana (712-713 CE, recorded by al-Tabari) and 9th-century CE Abbasid geographers (and conceivably 6th-century CE Chinese Si-kien).
b_akhsikath.etymology_analysis: Sogdian compound meaning 'town of the prince' (from axši- 'prince/ruler' + -kath 'town'), serving as the early medieval capital of Fergana on the Syr Darya.

b_khaylam.first_mention_attestation: Mid-10th-century CE Arabic geography Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 334) as Khaylam, and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 25, 59) as Khatlam, birthplace of the Samanid amir Nasr ibn Ahmad.

morphemes.translation: town and river name on the Naryn

b_khaylam.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic-era borough on the Naryn (Khaylam) river in eastern Fergana, first attested in 10th-century CE geographical works (al-Istakhri c. 951 CE).

b_najm.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources or standard 10th-century CE Islamic geographies of Fergana.
b_najm.etymology_analysis: Arabic noun najm ('star'), appearing as a barony name in Fergana without a documented pre-867 CE settlement attestation.

b_ardalankath.first_mention_attestation: Mid-10th-century CE Arabic geography by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 329) and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 25, 72) as Ardalankath, a borough in Shash/Ilaq bordering Fergana.
b_ardalankath.etymology_analysis: Sogdian settlement toponym ending in -kath ('town'), attested in 10th-century CE geographical treatises as the chief place of a cluster of boroughs in Shash/Ilaq.

b_kasan.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Tang Chinese chronicles (as Kesa / Gesai) and Xuanzang's 7th-century CE Fergana account (629 CE), as well as early 8th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (713 CE).

morphemes.translation: ancient fortified town (linked to Kushan / strong castle)

b_kasan.etymology_analysis: Ancient Fergana city name (modern Kosonsoy), historically linked by scholars to the Kushan ethnonym or an Eastern Iranian term for a fortified town/citadel.

b_varukh.first_mention_attestation: Early 16th-century CE memoir Baburnama (c. 1503-1504 CE) by Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur, listing Varukh (Barukh) as one of the four subdivisions of Isfara.

morphemes.translation: fortress or fortified settlement (from Old Iranian *vāra-)

b_varukh.etymology_analysis: Sogdian toponym Wārōx, derived by Pavel Lurje from Old Iranian *vāra- ('fortress'), though its earliest surviving written mention as a settlement is in the early 16th-century CE Baburnama.

b_isfara.first_mention_attestation: 8th-century CE historical account in al-Tabari (II, p. 1440) for 103 AH / 721-722 CE, recording Asfara as a rural district in Fergana where Sogdian emigrants were resettled.

morphemes.translation: district and town name in southern Fergana

b_isfara.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic and pre-Islamic Sogdian district name (Asfara/Espara), attested in al-Tabari for 721-722 CE and also borne by a local Sogdian prince of Fergana.

b_hoshyar.first_mention_attestation: Early 16th-century CE memoir Baburnama (c. 1503-1504 CE) by Babur, naming Hushyar alongside Isfara, Varukh, and Sokh as one of the four mountain divisions of Isfara.
b_hoshyar.etymology_analysis: Persian/Tajik toponym Hūshyār ('alert, watchful'), attested in the early 16th-century CE Baburnama as a mountain settlement in the Sokh-Isfara district.

b_khojand.first_mention_attestation: Late 7th-century CE Arab raid accounts (680 CE, repulsed) and early 8th-century CE Islamic conquest narratives (713 CE and 722 CE, recorded by al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari), alongside Sogdian attestations.

morphemes.translation: ancient city on the Syr Darya

b_khojand.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Sogdian city name (Khujand/Khojanda) at the mouth of the Fergana Valley, attested in Sogdian and early Islamic conquest sources from 680 CE onward.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek accounts of Alexander the Great's founding of Alexandria Eschate (329 BCE) near or on the site of Achaemenid Cyropolis.
older_name_by_867.notes: Hellenistic and Achaemenid predecessors at the Khujand site on the Syr Darya.

b_kend-i-badam.first_mention_attestation: Early 16th-century CE Timurid-era works Baburnama and Habib al-Siyar (c. 1500-1525 CE) under the Persian compound name Kand-i Badam ('almond city').
b_kend-i-badam.etymology_analysis: Persian-Sogdian compound meaning 'almond town/city' (modern Konibodom), expanding the older Sogdian name Kand with the Persian modifier -i Bādām in the late medieval period.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Early 8th-century CE Sogdian documents from Qal'a-yi Mugh (c. 710-722 CE) mentioning the settlement under the name Kand.
older_name_by_867.notes: Original Sogdian name (knδ, 'town') prior to the addition of the Persian qualifier '-i Badam'.

b_asht.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern ethnographic and administrative records of northern Tajikistan.

morphemes.translation: settlement and district name in northwestern Fergana

b_asht.etymology_analysis: Tajik/Iranian settlement and district name on the northern bank of the Syr Darya in Sughd, lacking a documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_wankath.first_mention_attestation: Mid-10th-century CE Arabic geography by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) as Wankath in Upper Nasaiya (Fergana), and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 25, 48) as Vathkath.
b_wankath.etymology_analysis: Sogdian settlement toponym ending in -kath ('town'), attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies as a border town between Khujand and Fergana.

b_afrasiyab.first_mention_attestation: Late 17th-century CE written sources (c. 1690 CE), where the ruined northern mound of Samarkand first appears under the name Qal'a-ye Afrasiab ('Castle of Afrasiab').

morphemes.translation: mythical Turanian king (folk-etymologized from 'beyond the black river')

b_afrasiyab.etymology_analysis: Popularly linked to the mythical king Afrasiyab of Iranian epic, but analyzed by scholars as a corruption of Persian Parsīāb / Sogdian Paršvāb ('beyond the black river', referring to the Siab stream).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek historians of Alexander the Great (329 BCE) recording the ancient Sogdian city as Marakanda.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient and early medieval urban core of Samarkand prior to the 17th-century CE 'Afrasiyab' designation.

b_andijan.first_mention_attestation: Late 10th-century CE Arabic geography Kitab Surat al-Ard by Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), referring to the town in Lower Nasaiya as Andukan.

morphemes.translation: eastern Fergana city name (traditionally linked to Turkic Andi/Adoq tribes)

b_andijan.etymology_analysis: Uncertain etymology; attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographers as Andukān/Andigān and traditionally linked to Turkic tribal names (Andi).

b_quba.first_mention_attestation: Mid-10th-century CE Arabic and Persian geographies of al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 25, 55) as Quba, a flourishing town in Fergana.
b_quba.etymology_analysis: Medieval Fergana town (modern Quva), variously explained from Persian qubā ('strong fortress') or a Turkic tribal name, first documented in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies.

b_khokand.first_mention_attestation: Mid-10th-century CE Arabic geographies of al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) as Khuvakand / Hawakand, and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 25, 54) as Khuwakand.
b_khokand.etymology_analysis: Sogdian/Iranian compound (*Hu-kand / Khuwākand) meaning 'good city', first attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works.

b_marghinan.first_mention_attestation: First attested by name as Marghinan in 10th-century Arabic geographies, notably al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), as a town in Lower Nasya; archaeological remains at the oasis date earlier, but the name itself is unattested <= 867 CE.
b_marghinan.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian/Sogdian toponym likely derived from margh ('meadow, pasture') with a toponymic suffix; popular legend deriving it from Persian murgh-i nān ('chicken and bread') is folk etymology.

b_sukh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Arabic and Persian geographies, including al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), Hudud al-Alam (982 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), as Sukh in Upper Nasya.
b_sukh.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Eastern Iranian/Sogdian oasis toponym (Sokh/Sukh) in southern Ferghana; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_aval.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Awal (capital of a mountainous district south of Margilan) in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE).

morphemes.translation: Aval (medieval Ferghana town and district name)

b_aval.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ferghana settlement and district name preserved in the modern village of Aval south of Margilan; exact linguistic root uncertain.

b_nasrabad.first_mention_attestation: Attested on a Samanid copper fals minted at Nasrabad in 340 AH (951 CE) and described by al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as a large town built for Nasr.
b_nasrabad.eponym_details: Named after the Samanid prince Nasr I ibn Ahmad (r. 864–892 CE), for whom his father Ahmad ibn Asad (d. 864/865 CE) built the town according to al-Muqaddasi.

morphemes.translation: victory (personal name of Samanid prince Nasr I)

b_nasrabad.etymology_analysis: Perso-Arabic compound ('settlement of Nasr'), founded by the Samanid governor Ahmad ibn Asad for his son Nasr I in the mid-9th century, though first attested in writing in the 10th century.

b_arslanbob.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; named in later local tradition after the 11th-century figure Arslanbob-Ata.
b_arslanbob.eponym_details: Named after Arslanbob-Ata (Arslanbab), an 11th-century Islamic saint and legendary walnut-grove founder in Ferghana.
b_arslanbob.etymology_analysis: Turkic-Arabic compound ('Lion Gate' or 'Elder Lion'), an eponymous toponym commemorating the 11th-century saint Arslanbob-Ata.

b_sarybulak.first_mention_attestation: No pre-modern written attestation found; modern Turkic/Kyrgyz settlement name.
b_sarybulak.etymology_analysis: Turkic hydronymic compound meaning 'yellow spring' (sary 'yellow' + bulak 'spring/stream'), common across Kyrgyzstan.

b_uzgend.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as Uzkand / Uzgand, and noted by Barthold as belonging in the 9th century to the Turkish prince Dihqan Chir-tagin.
b_uzgend.etymology_analysis: Turko-Sogdian hybrid toponym combining a Turkic first element (Öz/Uz) with the Sogdian urban suffix -kand ('town/settlement').

b_osh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 9th-century Arabic geographical works, notably Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE), as Ush, a major eastern Ferghana city.

morphemes.translation: Osh (ancient Ferghana city name, linked in scholarship to Vakhsh)

b_osh.etymology_analysis: Ancient Eastern Iranian settlement name; modern scholarship connects Osh with the river-goddess Vakhsh (Oxus) worshipped at Sulaiman-Too, though its exact derivation remains debated.

b_naqad.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE, as Nawqad) as a mountainous district in southern Ferghana.
b_naqad.etymology_analysis: Sogdian/Eastern Iranian compound meaning 'new settlement' (naw 'new' + kad/qad 'house/town').

b_miyan-rudan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Arabic geographies, including al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), as the district of Miyan-rudan between the Naryn and Qara-Darya rivers.
b_miyan-rudan.etymology_analysis: Persian regional choronym meaning 'between the rivers' (equivalent to Turkic Iki-su-arasi), designating the interfluve between the Naryn (Khaylam) and Qara-Darya.

b_darghan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Arabic geographies, including al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), as Darghan, the largest town on the left bank of the Amu Darya after Gurganj.

morphemes.translation: Darghan (medieval Khwarazmian town name of obscure origin)

b_darghan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian toponym of obscure origin, later known as Darghan-ata (modern Darganata).

b_tahiriya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) as Tahiriya, the southernmost town in Khwarazm five days' journey below Amul.
b_tahiriya.eponym_details: Named after the Tahirid dynasty (founded by Tahir ibn al-Husayn, d. 822 CE, or Abdallah ibn Tahir, d. 844 CE), governors of Khurasan.
b_tahiriya.etymology_analysis: Arabic dynastic toponym ('the Tahirid [station/town]') associated with the 9th-century Tahirid governors of Khurasan, though first attested in writing in the 10th century.

b_jigirbend.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) as Jiqarband (Jigarband) on the caravan route from Bukhara to Khwarazm, and later described by al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE).

morphemes.translation: Jigar (obscure toponymic element; literally 'liver/heart' in Persian)

b_jigirbend.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian-Persian compound ending in -band ('dam/embankment'), reflecting its position along the Amu Darya irrigation and caravan route.

b_sadvar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE, as Sadfar/Sadur) as a fortified town on the left bank of the Amu Darya.
b_sadvar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian town name (Sadwar/Sadvar), likely an Iranian compound with -wār ('enclosure/fortress').

b_ghardaman.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Ghardman, a fortified town with a moat one stage from Kath on the right-bank road.
b_ghardaman.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian settlement name attested in late 10th-century Arabic geography; exact root unestablished.

b_wayikhan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Waykhan, a fortified settlement with a moat on the right bank of the Amu Darya.
b_wayikhan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian settlement name attested in al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE); exact etymology uncertain.

b_gurganj.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by Ibn Fadlan (922 CE, as Jurjaniya) and al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, as Jurjaniya / Gurganj); the archaeological site dates back to the 5th century BCE.
b_gurganj.etymology_analysis: Khwarazmian toponym (Arabicized as Jurjaniya, later Turkicized as Urgench), analyzed by Yaqut as Gurgan + -j ('city/village').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: al-Tabari (recording Qutayba ibn Muslim's 712 CE campaign)
older_name_by_867.notes: In 712 CE, early Arabic histories record the left-bank breakaway principality and town of Khamjird in the vicinity of later Gurganj.

b_jith.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Git / Jit (Jith), a large fortified village on the left bank of the Amu Darya bordering the Oghuz.
b_jith.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian frontier settlement name (Git/Jit) attested in 10th-century Arabic geographies.

b_madminiya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) as Madhminiya and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Madhkaminiya, the northernmost settlement in Khwarazm.
b_madminiya.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian settlement name recorded in 10th-century Arabic geographical texts; exact root unknown.

b_urgench.first_mention_attestation: Modern Urgench (Uzbekistan) dates to the second half of the 19th century (following the 17th-century foundation of Taza Urgench); the Turkicized name form Urgench itself only appears from the 13th century onward.
b_urgench.etymology_analysis: Turkicized form of medieval Gurganj, transferred to the newer settlement of New Urgench in Uzbekistan after the Amu Darya shifted course.

b_vezir.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1464 CE by Mustafa Khan of the Golden Horde on the site of Devkesken Qala (per Barthold and Khwarazmian historiography).
b_vezir.etymology_analysis: Named after the Arabic administrative title wazīr ('vizier, minister'); founded in the 15th century as a late medieval capital of Western Khwarazm.

b_nazvar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Nuzwar (Nazvar), a small fortified village with iron gates on the left-bank road to Gurganj.
b_nazvar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian settlement name ending in -wār ('enclosure/fort'); attested in 10th-century Arabic geographies.

b_kath.first_mention_attestation: First attested by the name Kath (Kāṯ) in 10th-century Muslim geographies beginning with al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE); earlier sources refer to the citadel/city as Fir or Fil.
b_kath.etymology_analysis: Khwarazmian toponym explained by Yaqut as 'a rampart or mound in the steppe' and likely cognate with Sogdian kanṯ/kaṯ ('town, settlement').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arab-Sasanian coins (56 AH / 676 CE) and al-Tabari / al-Baladhuri (712 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Before the 10th century, the Afrighid capital and citadel on this site were known as Fir (or Fil) in 7th-century coinage and Arab conquest chronicles.

b_nukfagh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Nikfagh / Nukbagh (Nukfagh), a settlement on a canal off the Amu Darya one stage from Waykhan.
b_nukfagh.etymology_analysis: Khwarazmian compound likely meaning 'new garden/enclosure', attested in late 10th-century Arabic geography.

b_ardakhivah.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Ardakhiwa (Ardakhivah), a walled town at the foot of a mountain on the edge of the steppe.

morphemes.translation: upper, high, or sacred (cf. Avestan arəta-)

b_ardakhivah.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian compound sharing the second element of Khiva (Khīwaq) with an Iranian prefix arda- ('upper/sacred').

b_khiva.first_mention_attestation: Per Encyclopaedia Iranica, a settlement on the site existed by the 4th–3rd centuries BCE, but as a city it is first mentioned by 10th-century Arab geographers (al-Istakhri c. 951 CE, al-Muqaddasi c. 985 CE) as Khivaq.
b_khiva.etymology_analysis: Ancient Khwarazmian city name (historically Khīwaq), first attested in 10th-century Arabic geographical works.

b_rakhushmitan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Rakhushmithan / Ardakhushmithan, one day's journey from Kath.
b_rakhushmitan.etymology_analysis: Khwarazmian compound containing the Eastern Iranian suffix -mīthan ('dwelling, settlement'), attested in 10th-century Arabic geographies.

b_hazarasp.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by 10th-century Arabic geographers including al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE), though archaeological remains at the site date to the 1st millennium BCE.
b_hazarasp.etymology_analysis: Iranian compound meaning 'thousand horses', reflecting the strategic cavalry fortress at the southern gateway of Khwarazm.

b_karduran-khas.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Kardaran-Khas (Kardaran-Khwash), a fortified town three farsakhs from Hazarasp.
b_karduran-khas.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian compound town name attested in 10th-century Arabic geographical works.

b_kurdar.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Kardar (Kurdar) by al-Tabari (ii, 1525) under AH 110 (728/729 CE) as the residence of a local prince (malik), and later by Ibn Rusta (c. 903 CE), al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE).

morphemes.translation: Kurdar (early medieval Khwarazmian town and delta district name)

b_kurdar.etymology_analysis: Early medieval Khwarazmian town and delta district name attested in 8th-century historical accounts preserved by al-Tabari.

b_baratigin.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, as Faratagin) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE, as Baratagin), a large village near the Aral Sea.
b_baratigin.etymology_analysis: Likely a Turko-Iranian hybrid toponym containing the Turkic title tigīn ('prince'), attested in 10th-century Arabic geographies.

b_mizdahqan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by Ibn Rusta (c. 903–913 CE), al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Mizdakhqan; archaeological occupation at the nearby Gyaur-Kala fortress dates to the 4th–3rd centuries BCE.
b_mizdahqan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khwarazmian city and necropolis name; often linked in local and popular literature to Ahura Mazda, though its exact linguistic derivation remains unresolved.

b_north_kurdar.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation; modern geographical subdivision of the Kurdar district (repo res_name 'Amaliesburch' is an unrelated non-historical placeholder).
b_north_kurdar.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional label ('North Kurdar') applied to a barony slot in northern Kurdar; not a historical toponym.

b_zamakhshar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zamakhshar (زمخشر) in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works, notably al-Muqaddasi's Ahsan al-Taqasim (c. 985 CE), as a town in Khwarazm on the road to Gurganj.

morphemes.translation: medieval Khwarazmian town name (modern Izmukshir / Yzmykşir)

b_zamakhshar.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Khwarazmian settlement (archaeologically dated to the 3rd century BCE), whose name Zamakhshar is first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical literature and later Turkicized as Izmukshir / Yzmykşir.

b_ruzvand.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ruzwand / Rūzwand in al-Muqaddasi's Ahsan al-Taqasim (c. 985 CE) as a medium-sized town of Khwarazm between Uzarmand and Nuzwar.
b_ruzvand.etymology_analysis: Iranian/Khwarazmian toponym ending in the locative suffix -vand, recorded in 10th-century CE Arabic itineraries of Khwarazm (al-Muqaddasi).

b_chaghaniyan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (c. 646 CE, as Ch'ih-o-yen-na), in the Sogdian inscription on the Afrasiab murals at Samarkand (648–651 CE, as cγʾny / Chaganian), and in Tang annals (661 CE, as Che-han-na); later Arabicized as al-Saghaniyan.

morphemes.translation: local dynastic or regional root (uncertain pre-Islamic origin)

b_chaghaniyan.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym (Sogdian cγʾny, Middle Persian Čagīnīgān, Arabic Ṣaḡānīān); Encyclopaedia Iranica rejects earlier attempts to derive it from Mongolian čagan ('white').

b_termez.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xuanzang's 7th-century travelogue (c. 646 CE, as Ta-li-mi) and in early Islamic conquest chronicles (al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri) for the Umayyad campaigns of 676–704 CE as Tirmidh.

morphemes.translation: crossing place or on the river bank (proposed from Sanskrit tarmato)

b_termez.etymology_analysis: Ancient Oxus crossing-point attested in Chinese (Ta-li-mi) and early Arabic (Tirmidh) sources; scholars variously derive the name from Sanskrit tarmato ('on the river bank') or Greek thermos ('hot').

b_rigar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Rīkdasht / Rīgdasht in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE) as a settlement six farsakhs from the capital of Chaghaniyan.
b_rigar.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym (medieval Rīgdasht, modern Regar / Tursunzoda) meaning 'town on sand' or 'sandy plain'.

b_darzanji.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Darzanjī / Daranjī in al-Ya'qubi's Kitab al-Buldan (c. 891 CE) and 10th-century geographers (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi) as a weaving town in Chaghaniyan.
b_darzanji.etymology_analysis: Local Eastern Iranian / Persian toponym for a medieval weaving town on the Surkhan valley road between Termez and Chaghaniyan, first documented by al-Ya'qubi (891 CE).

b_basand.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Basand in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; al-Muqaddasi, c. 985 CE) as a large village with abundant gardens in Chaghaniyan.
b_basand.etymology_analysis: Local Eastern Iranian / Persian toponym for a fortified village in Chaghaniyan recorded by 10th-century CE geographers.

b_charmanjan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ṣarmanjān / Ṣarmanjī (Persianized Charmangān) in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE) six farsakhs north of Termez.

morphemes.translation: medieval town name between Termez and Chaghaniyan

b_charmanjan.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym (Arabicized Ṣarmanjān, Persianized Charmangān / Charmanjān) for a frontier ribat town in southern Chaghaniyan, first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies.

b_pargar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Parghar / Farghar (modern Farkhor) in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Hudud al-'Alam, 982 CE) as a town and river name in Khuttal.

morphemes.translation: settlement and river name in Khuttal

b_pargar.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym (medieval Parghar/Farghar, modern Farkhor/Parkhar) in southwestern Khuttal, first attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies.

b_hulbuk.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hulbuk (هلبك) in al-Ya'qubi's Kitab al-Buldan (c. 891 CE) and in 10th-century geographers (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Hudud al-'Alam, 982 CE) as the capital of Khuttal under the Banijurids.
b_hulbuk.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic / early medieval Eastern Iranian toponym for the seat of the rulers of Khuttal; although archaeological layers date to the 8th–9th centuries CE, the written name first appears in al-Ya'qubi (891 CE).

b_munk.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Munk in al-Ya'qubi's Kitab al-Buldan (c. 891 CE) and in 10th-century geographers (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Hudud al-'Alam, 982 CE) as the largest town in Khuttal.
b_munk.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym for the largest medieval town of Khuttal (near modern Khovaling / Baljuvon), first documented in al-Ya'qubi (891 CE).

b_rasht.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Rāsht (راشت) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) and in 9th–10th-century Islamic geographies as the mountain province and fortress corresponding to modern Karategin.
b_rasht.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym meaning 'red' (preserved in the Tajik name of the Surkhob river), attested in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) before being renamed Karategin in the 15th century.

b_shuman.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (c. 646 CE, as Su-man / Shu-man) and in al-Tabari's Tarikh for 705 CE (Qutayba ibn Muslim's campaign on behalf of Chaghaniyan against Shuman and Akharun).

morphemes.translation: medieval principality and fortress town in the upper Kafirnihan valley

b_shuman.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Eastern Iranian toponym for a principality and fortress town in the Hisor/Dushanbe basin, attested in 7th-century Chinese and early 8th-century Arabic sources.

b_vashjird.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Wāshjird / Wāshgird in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) and al-Ya'qubi's Kitab al-Buldan (891 CE) as a major frontier town in Khuttal.

morphemes.translation: toponymic root (associated in Persian tradition with Wīsa)

b_vashjird.etymology_analysis: Iranian compound toponym ending in -gird ('fortified town'), attested as Wāshjird in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) and corresponding to modern Vashgird in Tajikistan.

b_halavand.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Halāward (هلاورد) in al-Ya'qubi's Kitab al-Buldan (c. 891 CE) and in 10th-century geographers (al-Istakhri, Hudud al-'Alam) as the chief city of Wakhsh.
b_halavand.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym (medieval Halāward / Khelaverd, adapted as Halavand) for the capital of the Wakhsh valley, first attested in al-Ya'qubi (891 CE).

b_awzaj.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Awzaj / Awwāj in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE) as a river-crossing town where the Kafirnihan joins the Oxus.
b_awzaj.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym for a strategic Oxus river crossing at the mouth of the Kafirnihan (modern Ayvaj, Tajikistan), first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies.

b_qobadiyan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Xuanzang's 7th-century account (c. 646 CE, as Kio-ho-yen-na, identified with Kubadhiyan by Josef Markwart) and in al-Tabari's Tarikh for 725 CE during Asad ibn Abdallah's expedition to Khuttal.
b_qobadiyan.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian / New Persian toponym (Qubādhiyān / Qobādiyān) traditionally linked to Sasanian king Kavad I (r. 488–531 CE), attested in 7th-century Chinese and 8th-century Arabic historical accounts.

b_livkand.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lēwkand / Lāwkand in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE; Hudud al-'Alam, 982 CE) as a town on the Wakhsh River one day's journey above Halaward.
b_livkand.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian compound toponym ending in -kand ('town'), attested in 10th-century CE Arabic and Persian geographies of Wakhsh.

b_bunjiket.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Būnjikath / Bīnjikath in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as the capital of Ustrushana (archaeologically occupied from the 6th century CE).
b_bunjiket.etymology_analysis: Sogdian urban toponym ending in -kath ('town'), capital of the Principality of Ustrushana from the 6th to 9th centuries CE and documented in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).

b_bottaman.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Buttam / Buttamān in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan for early 8th-century CE Arab campaigns (c. 701–704 CE under Yazid ibn al-Muhallab) and in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) as the mountainous region between the upper Oxus and Syr Darya.

morphemes.translation: high mountain range (Hisar, Zarafshan, and Turkestan ranges)

b_bottaman.etymology_analysis: Sogdian and medieval Islamic oronym (Buttam / Buttamān) denoting the mountain ranges separating Sogdia and Ustrushana from the upper Oxus valleys.

b_dizak.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dīzak (ديزك) in al-Tabari's Tarikh (ii, 1439) for the early 8th-century CE campaigns in Ustrushana (722 CE) and in 10th-century geographies (al-Istakhri, Hudud al-'Alam).
b_dizak.etymology_analysis: Sogdian/Iranian diminutive toponym meaning 'small fortress' (modern Jizzakh, Uzbekistan), attested in al-Tabari's 8th-century narrative and 10th-century geographies.

b_zamin.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zāmīn in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as a major station on the highway from Samarkand to Khojend and Fergana.

morphemes.translation: earth, land, or border settlement name

b_zamin.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym (modern Zaamin, Uzbekistan) for the second-largest town of medieval Ustrushana, attested in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).

b_khawas.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Khāwas / Khawāṣ in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE) on the road from Zamin to Kurkath and the Syr Darya.
b_khawas.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym (modern Xovos, Uzbekistan) for a caravan station in northern Ustrushana, first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies.

b_kurkath.first_mention_attestation: The medieval form Kurkath (كركث) is first attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE) on the road from Khawas to Khojend.
b_kurkath.etymology_analysis: Sogdian evolution of Old Persian Kuruškaθa ('City of Cyrus', Greek Cyropolis); while the classical name is attested from the Achaemenid/Hellenistic era, the contracted medieval form Kurkath is first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Achaemenid foundation Kuruškaθa (c. 544 BCE) recorded in classical Greek and Latin histories (Arrian, Anabasis 4.3.1; Quintus Curtius Rufus 7.6.16).
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical and Old Persian names for the same settlement prior to the medieval Sogdian contraction Kurkath.

b_panjikand.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Pancyknδ (Panjikant) in the Sogdian documents from Mount Mugh (c. 722 CE) and in al-Tabari's account of the 722 CE Arab siege under Divashtich.
b_panjikand.etymology_analysis: Sogdian toponym Pancyknδ ('Five Towns' or 'Town of Panč'), attested in 8th-century CE Mount Mugh Sogdian documents and early Islamic chronicles.

b_barkat.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Barkath / Abarkath in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as a station four farsakhs from Samarkand on the road to Zamin and Khojend.
b_barkat.etymology_analysis: Sogdian toponym Barkath ('upper town'), chief settlement of the Buzmajan district northeast of Samarkand, attested in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).

b_varaghshar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Waraghsar / Varaghshar in 10th-century CE Islamic geographical works (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Hudud al-'Alam, 982 CE) as the site of the main headwater dam of Samarkand on the Zarafshan.
b_varaghshar.etymology_analysis: Sogdian hydraulic toponym Waraghsar meaning 'head of the dam' (modern Rabot-i Khoja / Dargom dam), first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic and Persian geographies.

b_bukhara.first_mention_attestation: Attested on indigenous Bukharan Sogdian coins modeled on Sasanian Bahram V (r. 420–438 CE) with the legend βwγʾr ('Bukhara'), in Xuanzang (c. 646 CE, as Pu-ho), and in al-Tabari for the 674 CE Arab campaign.

morphemes.translation: fortunate place (or possibly from Sanskrit vihāra, 'monastery')

b_bukhara.etymology_analysis: Sogdian toponym (*βuxārak, 'fortunate place', or alternatively derived from Buddhist Sanskrit vihāra, 'monastery'), attested on 5th-century CE Sogdian coinage and early Islamic histories.

b_varakhsha.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Narshakhi's Tarikh-i Bukhara (c. 943 CE) recording the killing of Bukhar Khudah Toghshada by Abu Muslim at Varakhsha around 753 CE, as well as in 10th-century geographies (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE).

morphemes.translation: ancient royal residence of the Bukhar Khudahs

b_varakhsha.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Sogdian toponym (also recorded as Farakhsha and Dakhfandun) for the ancient palace city of the Bukhar Khudahs northwest of Bukhara, archaeologically founded in the 1st century BCE.

b_ramitan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Narshakhi's Tarikh-i Bukhara (c. 943 CE) as Ramtin / Ramitan, noting that Abu Muslim stayed there during the Abbasid revolution (c. 747–755 CE) and that it was regarded as 'Old Bukhara'.
b_ramitan.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Sogdian toponym (Ramtin / Ramitan) in the Bukhara oasis, traditionally considered older than Bukhara itself and recorded in Narshakhi's account of the mid-8th century CE.

b_ghujduvan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Narshakhi's Tarikh-i Bukhara (c. 943 CE) as the hometown of a commander of the Sapid Jamagan (followers of al-Muqanna') during the 775–785 CE rebellion, and in 10th-century geographies (al-Istakhri, al-Muqaddasi).
b_ghujduvan.etymology_analysis: Iranian/Sogdian toponym (Ghujduwān / Ghijduwān) for a commercial town in the northern Bukhara oasis, attested in Narshakhi's account of the late 8th-century Sapid Jamagan uprising.

b_tavavis.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) and Narshakhi's Tarikh-i Bukhara (c. 943 CE), which records that the town received its Arabic name Dhat al-Tawawis ('place of peacocks', shortened to Tawawis) in 710 CE (91 AH).
b_tavavis.etymology_analysis: Arabic toponym meaning 'peacocks' (shortened from Dhāt al-Ṭawāwīs, 'place abounding in peacocks'), bestowed in 710 CE after Arab forces saw domesticated peacocks in the earlier Sogdian settlement of Arkud.

b_dabusiya.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Dabūsiyya in al-Tabari's Tarikh for the events of 728–729 CE, when only Samarkand, Kamarja, and Dabusiya remained in Arab hands during the Sogdian-Turgesh revolt.

morphemes.translation: medieval fortified town on the Zarafshan between Bukhara and Samarkand

b_dabusiya.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Sogdian fortified town (archaeologically occupied from the 3rd century BCE) on the Royal Road between Bukhara and Samarkand, attested in Arabic historiography from 728–729 CE.

b_kushaniya.first_mention_attestation: 554 CE (recorded in the Chinese Book of Wei as He [何], also called Kushuangnijia [屈霜你迦] / Guishangni [貴霜匿]; later attested in Xuanzang [646 CE], al-Tabari, and al-Istakhri)
b_kushaniya.etymology_analysis: From Sogdian Kūšānīk / Kushaniya, likely reflecting a Kidarite or Kushan-era royal foundation in western Sogdiana, rendered in Chinese chronicles as Kushuangnijia (屈霜你迦) and in Arabic as al-Kushaniya.

b_noor_bukhara.first_mention_attestation: 943–944 CE (described as Nur [Nur-i Bukhara] in Narshakhi's Tarikh-i Bukhara; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_noor_bukhara.etymology_analysis: Modern Nurota (Nurata), historically known as Nur or Nur-i Bukhara ('Light of Bukhara'). Local legend attributes the fortress and karez canals to Alexander the Great, but the name Nur is first attested in writing by Narshakhi in 943–944 CE.

b_kerminiya.first_mention_attestation: 943–944 CE (attested as Karminiya in Narshakhi's Tarikh-i Bukhara and in 10th-century Arabic geographers al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, and al-Muqaddasi; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)

morphemes.translation: large palace or residence (traditional Sogdian etymology)

b_kerminiya.etymology_analysis: Modern Karmana (Kermine) on the Zarafshan River. Traditional etymology derives Karmana from Sogdian meaning 'big palace'; Narshakhi (943 CE) also notes a local tradition that it was formerly called Badiya-i Khurdak ('little pitcher').

older_name_by_867.notes: Narshakhi (943 CE) mentions a traditional earlier name Badiya-i Khurdak, which itself lacks a pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_paykend.first_mention_attestation: 706 CE (conquest and sack of Paykend by Umayyad governor Qutayba ibn Muslim recorded in al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri, and Narshakhi)
b_paykend.etymology_analysis: From Sogdian Paykand (Arabic Baykand, Uzbek Poykent), a major pre-Islamic Sogdian merchant city southwest of Bukhara on the lower Zarafshan, containing the Sogdian element -kand ('town, fort').

b_firabr.first_mention_attestation: 867–870 CE (253–256 AH: Imam al-Bukhari taught Sahih al-Bukhari in Firabr, transmitted by Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Firabri [b. 845–846 CE]; also described in Qudama, al-Istakhri, and al-Muqaddasi)
b_firabr.etymology_analysis: Also rendered Farabr or Farab, a fortified crossing-town on the right (Transoxianan) bank of the Amu Darya opposite Amul (Charjuy), attested by 867 CE in connection with Imam al-Bukhari and his transmitter al-Firabri.

b_barzam.first_mention_attestation: 1072 CE (Barzam Fortress on the Amu Darya where Seljuk Sultan Alp Arslan was fatally wounded by Yusuf al-Khwarazmi in November 1072 CE; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_barzam.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress (Barzam / Barzem) near the Amu Darya in Khwarazm/Transoxiana, attested in Seljuk-era chronicles for the 1072 CE death of Alp Arslan.

b_nevida.first_mention_attestation: c. 985 CE (attested as Nawidah in al-Muqaddasi's Ahsan al-Taqasim as a crossing-town on the right bank of the Amu Darya; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_nevida.etymology_analysis: Medieval river-crossing town (Nawidah) on the right bank of the Amu Darya between Karkuh and Farabr, recorded by al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as the crossing used by travelers from Balkh to Samarkand.

b_kalif.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested as Kalif in 10th-century Arabic geographers al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, and al-Muqaddasi as a crossing-town on both banks of the Amu Darya; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)

morphemes.translation: fortified river crossing on the Oxus (modern Kelif)

b_kalif.etymology_analysis: Medieval crossing-point (Kalif / Kelif) on the Amu Darya between Balkh and Nakhshab, described in 10th-century Arabic geographies as straddling both banks of the river.

b_akhsisak.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested in al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, and al-Muqaddasi as a town on the right bank of the Amu Darya opposite Zamm/Kerki; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_akhsisak.etymology_analysis: Medieval Transoxianan town on the right bank of the Amu Darya facing Zamm (modern Kerki), forming a single administrative unit with Zamm in 10th-century Arabic geographies.

b_subakh.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested in al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, and al-Muqaddasi as a town in the Khuzar district on the road between Nasaf and Balkh; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)

morphemes.translation: medieval oasis town in the Khuzar (Guzar) basin

b_subakh.etymology_analysis: Medieval town in the Khuzar (Guzar) district of southern Sogdiana, identified by Barthold with modern Guzar on the main route between Nasaf and Balkh.

b_kishsh.first_mention_attestation: 636 CE (attested in the Book of Sui [Sui Shu] and Xuanzang's Great Tang Records [646 CE] as Kieshuangna [羯霜那] / Shi [史], on 7th-century Sogdian coins, and in al-Tabari for 7th–8th century Arab campaigns)

morphemes.translation: ancient Sogdian city name (traditional folk etymology 'heart-pleasing')

b_kishsh.etymology_analysis: From Sogdian *Kəš- (Keš / Kishsh), an ancient Iranian city in the upper Kashkadarya valley, renamed Shahrisabz ('Green City') in the Timurid period (14th century CE).

older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Nautaca (329 BCE) was a district/regional name in the Kashkadarya area, not a confirmed same-site name of Kesh.

b_kandak.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested in al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, and al-Muqaddasi as a mountain station one stage north of the Iron Gate [Dar-i Ahanin] and three stages from Kish; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_kandak.etymology_analysis: From Sogdian kand ('town, fort') with the Iranian diminutive suffix -ak ('little town'), a medieval road junction north of the Iron Gate pass.

b_al_musala.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested in 10th-century Arabic geographers al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal as al-Musalla, the extramural festival prayer ground outside Kish where the governor's palace stood; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_al_musala.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-muṣallā ('place of prayer'), referring to the extramural prayer ground outside the shahristan and rabad of Kish where the 10th-century governor's palace was situated.

b_nakhshab.first_mention_attestation: 775–783 CE (attested in al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri, and Narshakhi for the 8th-century Arab conquests and the revolt of al-Muqanna', the 'Moon-maker of Nakhshab'; Arabicized as Nasaf)

morphemes.translation: ancient Sogdian oasis city name (Arabicized as Nasaf)

b_nakhshab.etymology_analysis: Ancient Sogdian city in the lower Kashkadarya oasis, rendered by Arabs as Nasaf and later replaced by the 14th-century Mongol-era city name Qarshi ('palace').

b_nawqad_qureish.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested in al-Istakhri, al-Muqaddasi, al-Sam'ani, and Yaqut as Nawkad Quraysh / Nawqad-Quraysh between Kish and Nasaf; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_nawqad_qureish.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Sogdian-Arabic toponym meaning 'New Settlement of Quraysh', a large village/town on the road between Kish and Nasaf attested in 10th-century Arabic geographies.

b_ribat_malik.first_mention_attestation: 1078–1079 CE (fortified caravanserai built by Karakhanid ruler Shams al-Mulk Nasr ibn Ibrahim on the road between Samarkand and Bukhara; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_ribat_malik.eponym_details: Named after the Karakhanid ruler Shams al-Mulk Nasr ibn Ibrahim (r. 1068–1080 CE, titled al-Malik), who built the caravanserai in 1078–1079 CE.
b_ribat_malik.etymology_analysis: From Arabic/Persian Rabāṭ-i Malik ('Caravanserai of the King'), referring to its Karakhanid founder Shams al-Mulk Nasr ibn Ibrahim (1078–1079 CE).

b_bezda.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested as Bazda / Bazdah / Pazda in al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi, and Hudud al-'Alam [982 CE] six farsakhs west of Nasaf; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)

morphemes.translation: fortified medieval town near Nasaf (modern Pazli)

b_bezda.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortified town (Bazda / Pazda) in the Nasaf oasis, attested from the 10th century CE onward and famous for the Hanafi/Maturidi jurists of the al-Bazdawi (al-Pazdawi) family.

b_samarkand.first_mention_attestation: 329 BCE (attested as Marakanda [Μαράκανδα] in Greek accounts of Alexander the Great's conquest, and as sm'rknδh in Sogdian Ancient Letter II of 313 CE)
b_samarkand.etymology_analysis: From Sogdian Smārkanδh ('stone fort' or 'rock town'), rendered in Greek as Marakanda (329 BCE) and later folk-etymologized in Turkic as Sämizkänd ('fat city').

older_name_by_867.notes: Greek Marakanda (329 BCE) is an early classical transcription of the same Iranian name Samarqand.

b_arbinjan.first_mention_attestation: 699 CE (raid of Habib ibn al-Muhallab, followed by Qutayba ibn Muslim's 712 CE skirmish and Divashtich's 722 CE execution near Rabinjan, recorded in al-Tabari)
b_arbinjan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Sogdian town (Arbinjan or Rabinjan) on the Royal Road between Samarkand and Bukhara near modern Kattakurgan, attested in 7th–8th century Arab conquest narratives.

b_ishtikhan.first_mention_attestation: 636 CE (attested in the Book of Sui [Sui Shu] for 600–620 CE, in al-Tabari for 712–720 CE, in the New Book of Tang for 742 CE, and in al-Ya'qubi for the Ishtakhaniyya regiment in 836 CE)

morphemes.translation: Sogdian toponymic root (possibly 'eight' or local proper name)

b_ishtikhan.etymology_analysis: Important Sogdian town and principality northwest of Samarkand, which served as the residence of Sogdian ruler Gurak after 712 CE and gave its name to the 9th-century Abbasid Ishtakhaniyya regiment.

b_qatwan.first_mention_attestation: 1141 CE (site of the Battle of Qatwan on 9 September 1141 CE between the Qara Khitai and the Seljuks; also mentioned by al-Sam'ani in the 12th century; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_qatwan.etymology_analysis: Steppe plain north of Samarkand (between Warkath and Khushufaghn) famous for the decisive 1141 CE Battle of Qatwan.

b_wadhar.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (attested in al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal as a town north of Samarkand famous for cotton textiles; local mosque built by Suba' ibn al-Nadr, d. 882 CE; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)

morphemes.translation: medieval town north of Samarkand known for Wadhari cotton cloth

b_wadhar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Sogdian town two to four farsakhs north of Samarkand, settled by Arabs of the Bakr ibn Wa'il tribe and renowned in 10th-century sources for its high-quality cotton fabrics.

b_kurtysh.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Kurtysh is a desert locality along the upper Uzboy dry riverbed in Turkmenistan documented in 20th-century Soviet geographical surveys.

morphemes.translation: desert locality along the upper Uzboy channel

b_kurtysh.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen toponym for a locality along the upper Uzboy dry riverbed in northwestern Turkmenistan, appearing in 20th-century hydrological and archaeological literature.

b_bala_iskem.first_mention_attestation: c. 1885 CE (Bala-Ishem station opened on the Trans-Caspian Railway in western Turkmenistan; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_bala_iskem.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen settlement and railway station (Bala-Ishem) near the Bala-Ishem salt marshes southeast of Balkanabat, attested from the late 19th century.

b_igdy.first_mention_attestation: 1954 CE (archaeological discovery of the Parthian-era fortress of Igdy-Kala on the Uzboy by S. P. Tolstov; the Turkmen name Igdy has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)

morphemes.translation: Igdy (Turkmen tribal/locality name associated with the Uzboy)

b_igdy.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen locality name along the Uzboy River, famous for the nearby Parthian-Sasanian stone fortress of Igdy-Kala (discovered in 1954), whose ancient name is unattested in written sources.

b_nebit_dag.first_mention_attestation: 1933 CE (founded as Neftedag along the Trans-Caspian Railway, renamed Nebit-Dag in 1946 and Balkanabat in 2001; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_nebit_dag.etymology_analysis: From Turkmen Nebit-Dag ('Oil Mountain'), a Soviet-era petroleum town founded in 1933 as Neftedag at the foot of the Great Balkhan range and renamed Balkanabat in 2001.

b_cheleken.first_mention_attestation: 1715 CE (first mapped by Alexander Bekovich-Cherkassky as Chereken Island in the Caspian Sea; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_cheleken.etymology_analysis: From Persian Čahār-kān ('Four Mines/Riches', referring to its oil, ozokerite, salt, and mineral deposits), a Caspian peninsula (formerly island) in western Turkmenistan.

b_sarykamysh.first_mention_attestation: 1876 CE (first systematically charted by Russian geographer Nikolai Petrusevich; no documented written attestation of the name Sarykamysh <= 867 CE)
b_sarykamysh.etymology_analysis: From Turkic sary ('yellow') and kamysh ('reed'), denoting the large endorheic Sarygamysh Lake in northern Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

b_ortakuyu.first_mention_attestation: 1924 CE (documented as Orta-Kuyu, a Karakum Desert well/base during the 1924 Siege of Khiva campaign; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE)
b_ortakuyu.etymology_analysis: From Turkmen/Turkic Orta-Kuyu ('Middle Well'), a desert well in the Karakum Desert of Turkmenistan.

b_kugunek.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Kugunek is a locality along the upper Uzboy dry riverbed in Turkmenistan documented in 20th-century Soviet geographical surveys.

morphemes.translation: desert locality along the upper Uzboy channel

b_kugunek.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen toponym for a desert locality along the upper Uzboy dry riverbed in Turkmenistan, recorded in 20th-century hydrological surveys.

b_burgun.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Burgun is a modern village on the right bank of the Uzboy River in Bereket District, Balkan Province, Turkmenistan.

morphemes.translation: modern village on the Uzboy River in Balkan Province

b_burgun.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen village (Burgun obasy) on the right bank of the Uzboy River in Bereket District, western Turkmenistan.

b_dekcha.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Dekcha is a desert well and escarpment cape on the Ustyurt Plateau edge near the Uzboy in western Turkmenistan.

morphemes.translation: desert well and Ustyurt cape toponym

b_dekcha.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen toponym for a desert well (Kolodets Dekcha) and nearby Ustyurt escarpment cape in western Turkmenistan.

b_yashkan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Yaskhan (modern Ýasga) is a freshwater lake and village along the Uzboy River in Bereket District, Turkmenistan.

morphemes.translation: freshwater relict lake and settlement on the Uzboy

b_yashkan.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen toponym (Ýasga / Yaskhan) for a freshwater relict lake and village along the Uzboy channel in western Turkmenistan.
